assignments.title: 6.17 Primary Source Report: Declaration of Sentiments (1848)
assignments.html:
You have read the Declaration of Sentiments and studied how women won the vote. Write a report of 300 to 450 words. Use your own words except where you quote.

  1. What it claims. In two or three sentences, say what the writers at Seneca Falls were asking for and what they said was wrong.
  2. How it is built. The writers copied the shape of another famous document. Quote two short phrases from the Declaration of Sentiments that show this copying, and explain what the writers gained by borrowing from the Declaration of Independence.
  3. Connect it to the lesson. The 19th Amendment passed seventy-two years after Seneca Falls. Name two things the lesson says people did during those years, and explain what the delay tells you about how the republic changes its rules.
  4. What this source cannot tell you. Name one question about the movement that this document alone cannot answer, and say where you might look for the answer.

assignments.title: 6.37 Primary Source Report: The Sedition Act of 1798
assignments.html:
You have read the text of the Sedition Act of 1798 and studied how it was used. Write a report of 300 to 450 words. Use your own words except where you quote.

  1. What the law does. In two or three sentences, say what the Act made a crime and what the penalty was. Quote one short phrase from the law's text.
  2. Fair on paper? Find one feature of the text that Andrew Hamilton, Zenger's lawyer, would have welcomed, and one feature that he would have objected to. Explain each.
  3. Fair in use? Use the lesson to say who was tried under the Act, and what that tells you about how a law can be fair on paper and unfair in use.
  4. What this source cannot tell you. Name one question about how people at the time felt about the Act that the text alone cannot answer, and say where you might look for the answer.

assignments.title: 7.17 Primary Source Report: The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890)
assignments.html:
You have read the text of the Sherman Antitrust Act and studied how the republic answered the giant companies of the late 1800s. Write a report of 300 to 450 words. Use your own words except where you quote.

  1. What the law does. In two or three sentences, say what Sections 1 and 2 make illegal and what the punishment is. Quote one short phrase from the law’s text.
  2. Why a market needs it. Use Adam Smith’s passage and the lesson to explain how a monopoly keeps the “invisible hand” from working. Give one specific example from the lesson.
  3. Strong on paper, weak in use? Use the lesson to say how the Act was used in its first years, and how it was used against Standard Oil. What does this show about the difference between the words of a law and the way it is enforced?
  4. What this source cannot tell you. Name one question about the Act’s results, such as whether it made prices lower, that the text alone cannot answer, and say where you might look for the answer.

assignments.title: 8.7 Primary Source Report: Bush, Address to a Joint Session of Congress (2001)
assignments.html:
You have read part of President Bush’s address to Congress and studied how the nation answered the attacks of September 11. Write a report of 300 to 450 words. Use your own words except where you quote.

  1. What he says. In two or three sentences, say whom Bush names as the enemy and whom he says is not the enemy. Quote one short phrase from the speech.
  2. Safety and liberty. Use the lesson to name one action the nation took after the attacks that gave the government more power, and explain one reason a citizen might worry about it and one reason a citizen might support it.
  3. An earlier test. Compare Bush’s words about how Americans should treat one another with what happened to Japanese Americans in 1942. What does the comparison show about the difference between what a leader says and what a nation does?
  4. What this source cannot tell you. Name one question about how Americans actually treated one another after the speech that the text alone cannot answer, and say where you might look for the answer.

assignments.title: 9.17 Primary Source Report: The Declaration of Independence (1776)
assignments.html:
You have read part of the Declaration of Independence and studied the Enlightenment ideas and the British policies behind it. Write a report of 300 to 450 words. Use your own words except where you quote.

  1. What it says. In two or three sentences, say what the Declaration says is the purpose of government and where a government gets its power. Quote one short phrase from the text.
  2. A charge and a right. Choose one grievance from the list against the king. Use the lesson to say which policy it refers to and which natural right or principle it says was violated.
  3. Was the case fair? Name one reason a reader in 1776 might have thought this grievance was serious enough to justify independence, and one reason a loyal colonist might have disagreed. Use the lesson’s facts, such as the Olive Branch Petition.
  4. What this source cannot tell you. Name one question about the colonists that the text alone cannot answer, such as whether all of them supported independence, and say where you might look for the answer.

assignments.title: 10.27 Primary Source Report: Miranda v. Arizona (1966)
assignments.html:
You have read part of Chief Justice Warren’s opinion in Miranda v. Arizona and studied how the Bill of Rights applies to people accused of crimes. Write a report of 300 to 450 words. Use your own words except where you quote.

  1. What the Court requires. In two or three sentences, name two of the warnings that police must give a suspect before questioning, and say which amendment the Court is protecting. Quote one short phrase from the opinion.
  2. Why it matters. Use the lesson to explain how Miranda is connected to the Fifth and Sixth Amendments, and to the 14th Amendment, since Arizona is a state.
  3. Balancing safety and rights. Compare Miranda with Terry v. Ohio. In each case, what is the Court trying to balance, and how does it decide? Use one fact from each case.
  4. What this source cannot tell you. Name one question about how the ruling has worked in practice that the opinion alone cannot answer, and say where you might look for the answer.

quizzes.title: Module 6 Intro: The Citizen
quizzes.description:
In this module you will ask who counts as a citizen, what a citizen owes, how the vote widened, how a president is chosen, how citizens keep watch on power, and how a state and a nation share the work of governing. These questions come first so that you can see how your answers change by the end.

By the end of this module you will be able to:

  • explain how Americans have answered the question of who counts as a citizen, and what citizens owe;
  • describe how amendments widened the vote and how a vote is counted and an election is decided;
  • explain how juries, a free press, and informed citizens check the power of government;
  • describe how power is shared between the nation and the states, and how a citizen can act on a local problem.

questions.text: "What does a republic need from its citizens, and what do citizens need from their republic?" Answer in three or four sentences. There is no wrong answer yet. We will ask again at the end.
I have read the module goals above.

answers.text: Yes, I have read them.
I have a question about them. (Say what in the next question.)

questions.text: If you chose the second answer above, what is your question? Otherwise write "none."
Some assessments in this module may be done alone or with a group. If you choose a group, you will sign the Group Covenant first. Which would you like?

answers.text: I plan to work alone.
I would like to work in a group.
I am not sure yet.

quizzes.title: 6.2 Reading Quiz: Dred Scott to the 14th Amendment: Who Counts as a Citizen
quizzes.description: Five questions on how Americans have answered the question of who counts as a citizen.

questions.text: The 14th Amendment never names Dred Scott. What lets you conclude that it overturned Taney's view of citizenship?

answers.text: It was ratified after the Civil War by a Congress that disliked the Court.
It makes birth and naturalization the two roads to citizenship and names no race, so no one can be shut out as Taney said.
It banned slavery in the territories where Scott had lived.
It gave each state the power to decide who its citizens are.

questions.feedback_correct: Taney said no Black American could be a citizen. The amendment's first sentence names no race, and it makes national citizenship come first, so a state cannot shut out the nation's citizens.

questions.text: Wong Kim Ark's parents could not be naturalized, yet the Supreme Court said he was a citizen. Which reasoning best explains the decision?

answers.text: His parents became citizens while he was away in China.
The Chinese Exclusion Act had been struck down.
His birth on American soil made him a citizen, whatever his parents' status.
The Court decided that the 14th Amendment did not apply to children.

questions.feedback_correct: The rule of birth held. The decision protected every child born here, whatever the nation of the parents.

questions.text: The lesson says a Court with more restraint "might have spared the country" the decision in *Dred Scott*. What does that suggest about what the Court did?

answers.text: It answered the biggest question it could when it could have ruled more narrowly.
It ruled on a question that the Constitution forbids courts to answer.
It followed a plan that every justice had agreed on from the start.
It ruled for Dred Scott but gave no reasons.

questions.feedback_correct: Some justices wanted a narrow ruling. The Court chose the widest answer, and it made the two sides angrier.

questions.text: People born in American Samoa are U.S. nationals, not automatic citizens. What does this show about citizenship?

answers.text: Anyone born under the American flag is a citizen with no exceptions.
Nationals owe no loyalty to the United States.
Puerto Rico and American Samoa were treated in exactly the same way.
Citizenship in the territories is still set by Congress and the courts.

questions.feedback_correct: Congress made Puerto Ricans citizens by a law in 1917, but did not do the same for American Samoa.

questions.text: The Chinese Exclusion Act was passed after the 14th Amendment. What does the pairing of the two show?

answers.text: A country can write a generous rule for birth and still be stingy about who may join.
The 14th Amendment was repealed when the Act passed.
Congress has no power over immigration.
Chinese immigrants were granted naturalization soon after.

questions.feedback_correct: The Act stopped Chinese workers from coming and said Chinese immigrants could not be naturalized, while birth on American soil still made a person a citizen.

quizzes.title: 6.4 Critical Questions: Taney, Dred Scott
quizzes.description: Two questions on Chief Justice Taney's opinion. Read the source first.

questions.text: Taney asks whether a person descended from enslaved Africans can be "a member of the political community" formed by the Constitution. What is he really deciding?

answers.text: Whether Dred Scott had been treated kindly by his owner.
Whether Congress may tax the territories.
Whether a Black American could ever be a citizen with the right to sue in federal court.
Whether the Constitution could be amended.

questions.feedback_correct: Taney's answer on citizenship decided that Scott could not bring his case at all.

questions.text: Which two statements fit the way Taney argues in this passage?

answers.text: He treats the framers' views as fixed, and says the Constitution must be read as they supposedly saw it.
He rests his case on the 14th Amendment.
He takes a very wide question, not just Scott's own case, and answers it for the whole nation.
He relies on the opinion of the enslaved men and women of the time.

questions.feedback_correct: The 14th Amendment did not yet exist, and Taney does not use the views of enslaved people.

quizzes.title: 6.7 Reading Quiz: Duties and Responsibilities: Jury, Draft, and Virtue
quizzes.description: Five questions on what the law requires of citizens and what a free republic hopes they will choose to do.

questions.text: A man pays his taxes and registers for Selective Service. He never votes and never reads about problems in his town. Which description fits him best?

answers.text: He has broken the law.
He is doing everything a good citizen should do.
He keeps his obligations but neglects his responsibilities.
He has lost the rights of a citizen.

questions.feedback_correct: Taxes and registration are obligations the law requires. Voting and staying informed are responsibilities a good citizen chooses.

questions.text: Why does the lesson say jury service shows what a citizen really is?

answers.text: It lets ordinary citizens share directly in ruling by deciding the facts of a case.
It is the one duty that people who are not citizens also owe.
It takes the place of voting for people who are called.
It gives lawyers and judges a break from their work.

questions.feedback_correct: On a jury, ordinary citizens decide the facts, in the courthouse and not in the capital.

questions.text: Washington could have stayed President for life, but he stepped aside after two terms. What does the lesson want you to take from this?

answers.text: He expected to lose the next election.
The Constitution barred a third term in 1796.
He was too ill to continue.
A republic needs leaders who can walk away, and no law forced him to do it.

questions.feedback_correct: The law did not force him to go. A good citizen chose to, and later Presidents followed his habit for almost 150 years.

questions.text: Washington called religion and morality "indispensable supports" of a free government. According to the lesson, what did he think would happen if a people lost honesty and the habit of keeping promises?

answers.text: They would need no government at all.
They would need a strong ruler to keep order, and then they would no longer be free.
They would grow richer, because they would no longer follow rules.
They would be protected by the courts from the results.

questions.feedback_correct: A people without these habits needs a strong ruler to keep order.

questions.text: A friend says, "If it isn't against the law, it isn't my business." Which idea from the lesson answers him best?

answers.text: Laws apply only to citizens who were born here.
Responsibilities are only for people who plan to run for office.
Responsibilities are the true test of character, because when you ignore one, only the community suffers.
A citizen who obeys the law has already done everything a republic needs.

questions.feedback_correct: Anyone will do what the law forces. The question is what a person does when the law is silent.

quizzes.title: 6.8 Critical Questions: Washington, Farewell Address
quizzes.description: Two questions on Washington's parting advice. Read the source first.

questions.text: Washington calls religion and morality "indispensable supports" of political prosperity. Which sentence best states his reasoning?

answers.text: Laws alone cannot hold a free people together, so their character has to do part of the work.
A free people needs no laws if everyone is religious.
Only the President is expected to be moral.
Morality matters in private life but not in government.

questions.feedback_correct: He treats virtue as a "necessary spring" of popular government.

questions.text: Washington writes this advice as someone who wants to keep power. True or false?

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: He wrote it as he left office by choice, after two terms, so he gained nothing by saying it.

quizzes.title: 6.12 Reading Quiz: Amending the Constitution: The 13th, 14th, and 15th
quizzes.description: Five questions on how the Constitution is amended and how three amendments after the Civil War widened the republic.

questions.text: The lesson calls Article V "a middle path." What does that mean?

answers.text: The President alone may change the Constitution when Congress agrees.
Congress may amend it by a simple majority of both houses.
Every state must agree before any change is made.
It is hard enough to protect the Constitution from passing moods, and open enough that a determined people can still change it.

questions.feedback_correct: The Framers remembered the Articles of Confederation, where every state had to agree, and they chose something in between.

questions.text: The House passed the 13th Amendment by 119 to 56, only a handful of votes more than the two-thirds it needed. Why does the lesson stress how close this was?

answers.text: If the House had failed again, the question would have waited for a new Congress and the war might have ended in a different way.
The President had to sign the amendment, and he was not sure he would.
A close vote means the amendment was not legal.
The Senate had already voted against it.

questions.feedback_correct: The Senate had already passed it. A failed vote would have pushed the question to the next Congress.

questions.text: The lesson says the words of the 14th Amendment about due process and equal protection "aimed at the Black Codes." What can you infer about why Congress wrote them?

answers.text: Congress wanted to give the states more power over freed people.
Congress wanted to make the Constitution shorter.
Congress wanted to stop states from taking rights away from freed people, and it made the amendment bind the states.
Congress wanted to end the war.

questions.feedback_correct: The Black Codes were state laws, so the amendment was written to limit what states may do.

questions.text: The 15th Amendment says the vote cannot be denied "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude." Why could Southern states still use poll taxes and literacy tests?

answers.text: The Supreme Court had ruled the amendment did not apply to the South.
The amendment banned denying the vote because of race, and the poll tax and literacy test laws did not mention race.
Poll taxes were required by the 14th Amendment.
Federal troops enforced these laws.

questions.feedback_correct: The laws did not say "Black." Officials gave the tests unfairly, the fees were too high for many poor families, and violence did the rest.

questions.text: What do the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments together teach about how the republic widened?

answers.text: The nation widened the republic by using Article V, and each step was hard won.
The nation widened the republic by setting aside the Constitution during Reconstruction.
The nation widened the republic only by court decisions.
The nation widened the republic quickly, because Article V is easy to use.

questions.feedback_correct: The nation did not tear up the Constitution. It used the road the Framers built.

quizzes.title: 6.14 Critical Questions: The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments
quizzes.description: Two questions on the text of the three Reconstruction Amendments. Read the source first.

questions.text: The 13th Amendment bans slavery "except as a punishment for crime." What does this exception teach you about reading a legal text?

answers.text: The amendment ended slavery everywhere, with no exceptions.
It applied only to the states that had left the Union.
Its authors wrote it to protect slaveholders.
The exact words matter, because a clause can leave room for something the main sentence seems to forbid.

questions.feedback_correct: The exception allows forced labor as punishment for a crime, so the sentence does not mean "no one can ever be forced to work."

questions.text: Which two phrases show a limit placed on what a state may do?

answers.text: "No State shall make or enforce any law which shall abridge the privileges or immunities of citizens"
"All persons born or naturalized in the United States"
"nor deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws"
"shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction"

questions.feedback_correct: Both phrases begin by naming the State as the one who may not act.

quizzes.title: 6.18 Critical Questions: Declaration of Sentiments
quizzes.description: Two questions on the document written at Seneca Falls. Read the source first.

questions.text: The authors copy the opening of the Declaration of Independence but change "all men" to "all men and women." Why would they borrow the nation's own words?

answers.text: To argue that the country's founding promise already demands the rights they want.
To show that the Declaration of Independence was a mistake.
To ask the British to rule America again.
To avoid saying anything new.

questions.feedback_correct: They hold the nation to its own principles.

questions.text: The Declaration of Sentiments asks the nation to give up its founding ideas about rights.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: It asks the nation to live up to those ideas.

quizzes.title: 6.22 Reading Quiz: How We Vote: Local, State, National
quizzes.description: Five questions on who runs elections, who may hold office, and how the census changes the House.

questions.text: Under the Elections Clause, each state decides the "times, places and manner" of holding elections for Congress. Why would the Framers have set it up this way?

answers.text: They expected the President to run elections later.
They believed states were better at counting ballots than Congress.
They did not want one central power to control how the people choose their rulers.
They wanted to give local officials the power to decide who may vote.

questions.feedback_correct: Congress may still change the rules, but states and local officials run nearly every election.

questions.text: A House member must be 25, a Senator 30, and a President 35 and natural-born. What can you infer about the Framers' thinking?

answers.text: They wanted the highest offices held by people with more years of experience and a long tie to the country.
They thought young people should never take part in government.
They wanted the House to be the most powerful body.
They had no particular reason for the differences.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson says the Senate was meant to be steady and experienced, and the President needed even more years behind him. The natural-born rule came from a fear of foreign influence.

questions.text: The House has been fixed at 435 seats since 1929. In 1950 Florida had eight seats and now has twenty-eight. What must be true?

answers.text: The House grew by twenty seats.
Florida has more Senators than it used to.
Florida now elects the President.
Other states must have gained fewer seats or lost seats, because a state can gain one only if another loses one.

questions.feedback_correct: With the total fixed, each census starts a new contest over a limited number of chairs.

questions.text: Why does it matter that American voting is secret?

answers.text: It lets officials count ballots faster.
No boss or neighbor can punish you for the way you voted, because nobody may force you to show it.
It makes registration unnecessary.
It prevents any candidate from losing.

questions.feedback_correct: Secrecy protects the citizen's free choice.

questions.text: The lesson calls the census "a map of power that is redrawn every ten years." Why?

answers.text: It tells the President who his friends are.
It counts only the citizens who voted in the last election.
It sets the number of House seats for each state, which also affects votes in the Electoral College.
It decides which party will win the next election.

questions.feedback_correct: Seats in the House help decide each state's electoral votes. The census counts everyone who lives in the country, not only citizens or voters.

quizzes.title: 6.24 Critical Questions: Article II and the 12th Amendment
quizzes.description: Two questions on how the Constitution sets up the choice of a President. Read the source first.

questions.text: Under Article II, each state legislature decides how that state's electors are chosen.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: The text says each State appoints electors "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct."

questions.text: What did the 12th Amendment change about the way electors voted?

answers.text: It let the voters choose electors directly.
It made electors name one person for President and a separate person for Vice President.
It raised the number of electors for each state.
It ended the use of electors.

questions.feedback_correct: The text calls for "distinct ballots," which answers the tie that happened in 1800.

quizzes.title: 6.27 Reading Quiz: The Electoral College and the Election of 1800
quizzes.description: Five questions on how the Electoral College works and how the election of 1800 was settled.

questions.text: Why did Jefferson and Burr tie with 73 votes each in 1800?

answers.text: Burr had won more states than Jefferson.
Each elector cast two votes without saying which was for President, and every Republican elector voted for both men.
The House had already voted and split the result.
Adams had dropped out of the race.

questions.feedback_correct: The Republicans won, but because the ballots did not separate the two offices, the winners tied.

questions.text: How did the 12th Amendment keep a tie like that of 1800 from happening by accident again?

answers.text: It gave the Senate the power to choose the President.
It ended the use of electors.
It said that a tie goes to the Supreme Court.
It had electors cast one ballot for President and a separate ballot for Vice President.

questions.feedback_correct: If no one wins a majority, the House still decides among the top candidates, and the Senate chooses the Vice President.

questions.text: Hamilton disliked Jefferson but urged Federalists to choose him over Burr. What does this show?

answers.text: He put the safety of the republic ahead of his own feelings.
He had changed his mind about Jefferson's ideas.
He had been promised a job by Jefferson.
He wanted the House to vote forever.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson calls this civic virtue at work: a leader helped the other side win because he feared worse for the country.

questions.text: Hamilton argued in Federalist No. 68 that a small group of electors would judge better than a crowd. What danger were the Framers trying to guard against?

answers.text: Voters who lived too far from the capital.
A President who served too many terms.
A clever speaker who could stir up the people with anger or tricks and win the office.
A President who was not an American citizen.

questions.feedback_correct: They had seen how a clever speaker could lead a crowd, and they wanted a check on that danger.

questions.text: The lesson says Adams left Washington before Jefferson's ceremony and compares this with Sulla and Caesar. What is the comparison meant to show?

answers.text: In America power changed hands without soldiers, because many people, including the loser, chose to accept the result.
Rome had a stronger army than America.
American leaders were more afraid of soldiers than Roman leaders were.
Adams had been forced out by the House.

questions.feedback_correct: The transfer of power was not guaranteed. It happened because people chose to accept the result.

quizzes.title: 6.28 Critical Questions: Jefferson, First Inaugural Address
quizzes.description: Two questions on Jefferson's first words as President. Read the source first.

questions.text: Jefferson says, "We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists." What is he trying to do?

answers.text: Announce that the two parties are being abolished by law.
Give his own party all the jobs in the government.
Say that the Federalists had been right all along.
Calm a bitter election by reminding both sides that they share the same basic principles.

questions.feedback_correct: He says "every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle."

questions.text: Which two ideas does Jefferson say a free republic must hold together?

answers.text: The will of the majority should prevail, if it is reasonable.
The minority has equal rights that the law must protect.
The winning party should decide what the minority may say.
Elections should be decided by the House alone.

questions.feedback_correct: He pairs majority rule with protection of the minority.

quizzes.title: 6.32 Reading Quiz: The Zenger Trial: Juries and the Press
quizzes.description: Five questions on the Zenger trial and the way a jury trial works.

questions.text: Under the rules of the court in 1735, why should Zenger's trial have been over before it began?

answers.text: Zenger had already confessed to treason.
The governor had chosen the jury himself.
Truth was the only defense allowed, and Zenger could not prove it.
The jury was asked only whether he printed the words, and everyone knew he had.

questions.feedback_correct: The judge decided whether the words were libel. The jury decided only who printed them.

questions.text: Andrew Hamilton admitted that Zenger printed the words. What did he then ask the jurors to do that the judge told them not to do?

answers.text: Decide that the printer was too poor to be tried.
Look beyond who printed the words and consider whether they were true and whether a person should be punished for printing the truth.
Wait until a higher court could hear the case.
Find the judge guilty of libel.

questions.feedback_correct: The jury came back with "not guilty" after a short time.

questions.text: What does the verdict show about the jury as a check on government?

answers.text: Ordinary citizens with no reason to please the governor can refuse to convict when the government's case is unjust.
Juries must always obey the judge.
Juries are meant only to help judges save time.
Only experts can serve on a jury.

questions.feedback_correct: The jury was made of neighbors who knew what it was like to live under a governor like Cosby.

questions.text: The lesson says a paper that may print only praise "is not a window. It is a mirror held up by the government." What does that mean?

answers.text: A paper should show readers pictures instead of words.
A government should print its own paper in every town.
It shows rulers what they want to see, and citizens cannot learn what the rulers are really doing.
A newspaper that praises the government is always telling the truth.

questions.feedback_correct: Citizens cannot judge their rulers if they cannot learn what the rulers are doing.

questions.text: A prosecutor has weak evidence against a person. At which step could ordinary citizens first stop the case from going forward?

answers.text: When the judge sentences the accused.
When a grand jury decides whether there is enough evidence to go to trial.
When the accused proves he is innocent.
When the verdict is read.

questions.feedback_correct: The grand jury hears the evidence first. Later, the trial jury must be unanimous and the government carries the burden of proof.

quizzes.title: 6.34 Critical Questions: Andrew Hamilton, Defense of Zenger
quizzes.description: Two questions on Hamilton's words to the jury. Read the source first.

questions.text: Hamilton says this is "not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone." What point is he making to the jury?

answers.text: Zenger has no chance of being found guilty.
The verdict will decide whether anyone can speak and write the truth against those in power.
The jury must punish the printer to protect New York.
The governor should be put on trial instead.

questions.feedback_correct: He asks the jury to see the larger cause: "the liberty both of exposing and opposing arbitrary power."

questions.text: Hamilton tells the jury that the only question they must decide is whether Zenger printed the papers.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: He urges them to look beyond that and to weigh the truth of the words and the cause of liberty.

quizzes.title: 6.38 Critical Questions: The Sedition Act of 1798
quizzes.description: Two questions on the text of the Sedition Act. Read the source first.

questions.text: The Act punishes writing that is "false, scandalous and malicious." Why might critics say these words give the government too much power?

answers.text: They apply only to lies told under oath.
They require a jury of printers.
They let officials in power decide which criticism counts as scandalous.
They make every newspaper illegal.

questions.feedback_correct: The word "scandalous" can fit any strong criticism, and those who are criticized decide.

questions.text: According to Section 3, a person charged under the Act could use the truth of what he published as a defense.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: The text says the defendant may "give in evidence in his defence, the truth of the matter," which is the principle Hamilton argued for in the Zenger trial.

quizzes.title: 6.42 Reading Quiz: Federalism: States and the Nation
quizzes.description: Five questions on how power is shared between the nation and the states and how North America is divided.

questions.text: Madison wrote that the national government's powers are "few and defined" and the states' are "numerous and indefinite." Which job would he expect the states, and not the nation, to handle?

answers.text: Defending the country against an invasion.
Making treaties with foreign countries.
Running local schools and building local roads.
Printing the nation's money.

questions.feedback_correct: The nation handles a short list of large tasks. The states handle most of daily life.

questions.text: You win a lawsuit in Georgia and then collect the money from the loser in Florida. Which rule in Article IV makes this possible?

answers.text: Full faith and credit, which requires each state to respect the court judgments of the others.
Privileges and immunities, which gives you the right to vote in Florida.
The admission of new states.
The guarantee of a republican form of government.

questions.feedback_correct: A court judgment from one state must be respected in the others.

questions.text: The lesson says a state can try a new idea. Why can that help the whole country?

answers.text: It lets the state ignore the national Constitution.
It allows the nation to take credit for the idea.
It makes every state use the same idea.
If the idea fails the harm stays small, and the rest of the country learns from it.

questions.feedback_correct: This was one of the Framers' reasons for choosing self-government close to home.

questions.text: The nation guarantees every state a republican form of government. What is the point of this promise?

answers.text: It lets Congress run the states' elections.
No state could turn itself into a kingdom while it remains in the union.
It lets the President replace state governors.
It makes all states pass the same laws.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson calls this the republic's protection of itself.

questions.text: Why does the lesson say federalism fits a country like America?

answers.text: It requires every region to have the same laws.
It keeps the nation from having any borders.
Places with different land, work, and history will often want different laws, and federalism lets each state solve its own problems while the nation holds them together.
It lets the regions separate when they disagree.

questions.feedback_correct: A rule that suits a farming state may not suit a harbor city.

quizzes.title: 6.44 Critical Questions: Madison, Federalist No. 45
quizzes.description: Two questions on Madison's sorting of powers. Read the source first.

questions.text: According to Madison, which level of government will handle most of the ordinary matters of people's lives?

answers.text: The federal government, because its powers are "numerous and indefinite."
The state governments, because their powers extend to the lives, liberties, and properties of the people.
Neither, because the people handle these matters alone.
Both equally, with no difference between them.

questions.feedback_correct: Madison says the reserved powers of the states cover the ordinary course of affairs.

questions.text: Which two matters does Madison name as federal powers, used mainly on "external objects"?

answers.text: War
Local schools
Foreign commerce
The internal order of a state

questions.feedback_correct: Madison lists "war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce."

quizzes.title: 6.47 Reading Quiz: Florida's Constitution, Sources of Law, and Local Problems
quizzes.description: Five questions on Florida's constitution, the kinds of law, and how a citizen can act on a local problem.

questions.text: Article I of Florida's constitution lists the rights of the people before it says anything about the government. What does that order suggest?

answers.text: The people's rights come before the government does.
Florida's government has no limits.
The Legislature wrote the rights last.
Rights matter less than the courts.

questions.feedback_correct: The national Constitution put its list in amendments, after the rest.

questions.text: A law says restaurants must be clean. An agency then writes the rules for how often a kitchen must be inspected. What kind of law are the inspection rules?

answers.text: A constitution.
Case law, made by a judge.
A regulation, a rule written by an agency to carry out a statute.
A statute passed by the Legislature.

questions.feedback_correct: The statute sets the goal, and the agency writes the details.

questions.text: A driver causes a crash. He is charged with a crime and also sued for the damage. What does this show?

answers.text: The courts made a mistake.
One event can lead to both criminal and civil law.
Civil law is only for crimes against the state.
Only the federal government can bring charges.

questions.feedback_correct: The crime is the government's charge. The lawsuit is a dispute between people about who must pay.

questions.text: The lesson says a person who calls the President about a pothole "will wait a long time." Why does the lesson begin the four steps with knowing who provides what?

answers.text: Potholes are never fixed.
Only the President can help with local problems.
Local agencies do not take calls.
A citizen who knows which level has the power can take the problem to the right door.

questions.feedback_correct: Local governments provide services like police, fire protection, schools, and water. States build roads and run courts.

questions.text: Why does the lesson say a small group that attends a meeting often matters more than a large group that stays home?

answers.text: Meetings only count votes.
Officials hear most from the people who show up.
Large groups are not allowed to speak.
Small groups have more money.

questions.feedback_correct: Taking part is how a citizen's voice reaches the agency.

quizzes.title: 6.48 Critical Questions: Florida Constitution, Article I
quizzes.description: Two questions on Florida's Declaration of Rights. Read the source first.

questions.text: Section 1 says "All political power is inherent in the people." What does this tell you about where government gets its authority?

answers.text: From the Governor, who hands it to the people.
From the federal government, which grants it to the state.
From the people, so government is their servant and not their master.
From the courts, which decide who may rule.

questions.feedback_correct: It echoes the Declaration of Independence's "consent of the governed."

questions.text: Section 2 says that these basic rights belong to men only.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: It says "female and male alike."

quizzes.title: Module 6 Outro: The Citizen
quizzes.description: You have finished this module. Answer honestly. Your answers help your teacher see what is clear and what is not.

quizzes.title: Module 7 Intro: Money and Markets
quizzes.description:
In this module you will ask how a young nation borrowed money and kept its credit, how it raised taxes without losing its citizens, how a market works and what a republic does when one business grows too big, and what happened in nations that planned the whole economy. These questions come first so that you can see how your answers change by the end.

By the end of this module you will be able to:

  • explain what credit is and how Hamilton’s plan and the national bank built the new nation’s trust;
  • describe the kinds of taxes, why the whiskey tax led to rebellion, and how Washington answered;
  • explain how a market economy works, what a mixed economy is, and why a republic regulates monopolies;
  • compare market and command economies, and use GDP per capita as evidence while naming what it leaves out.

questions.text: Essential question, first answer. "How should a free republic handle money, markets, and the power of wealth?" Answer in three or four sentences. There is no wrong answer yet. We will ask again at the end.
Objectives. "I have read the module goals above."

answers.text: Yes, I have read them.
I have a question about them. (Say what in the box below.)

questions.text: Question about the goals. If you chose the second answer above, what is your question? Otherwise write "none."
Group work. "Some assessments in this module may be done alone or with a group. If you choose a group, you will sign the Group Covenant first. Which would you like?"

answers.text: I plan to work alone.
I would like to work in a group.
I am not sure yet.

quizzes.title: 7.2 Reading Quiz: Hamilton’s Debt Plan and the Bank
quizzes.description: Five questions on credit, Hamilton’s plan to pay the nation’s debts, and the fight over the national bank.

questions.text: Why does the lesson say that credit is built on trust?

answers.text: A lender must like the borrower personally.
A lender hands over money now and must believe the borrower will pay it back later.
The government guarantees every loan.
A trusted borrower never has to pay interest.

questions.feedback_correct: A borrower with a record of not paying back will find that lenders refuse, or ask for very high interest.

questions.text: What was Hamilton’s main argument for paying the national debt in full?

answers.text: The debt made the nation poor, so it should be wiped away.
France demanded payment at once.
Only the states should have to pay.
A nation that keeps its word will be trusted, and a trusted nation can borrow when it must.

questions.feedback_correct: Hamilton wanted the republic to have good credit for emergencies such as a war.

questions.text: What was the bargain of 1790?

answers.text: Madison and other Virginians let the assumption of state debts pass, and in return the capital was placed on the Potomac River.
Hamilton dropped the national bank, and Jefferson agreed to pay the debt.
Congress cancelled the war debt, and the states agreed to a tariff.
Jefferson became Treasury Secretary, and Hamilton became Secretary of State.

questions.feedback_correct: Washington, D.C. came out of that bargain.

questions.text: Jefferson said the Constitution does not give Congress the power to charter a bank. How did Hamilton answer?

answers.text: The Preamble promises liberty to the people.
The Tenth Amendment gives that power to the states.
The Constitution lets Congress make all laws that are “necessary and proper” for carrying out its listed powers, such as borrowing money.
President Washington had already approved the bank.

questions.feedback_correct: This was the first great argument about how broadly to read the Constitution.

questions.text: What does the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation do?

answers.text: It prints the nation’s money.
It is an agency that insures the money people put in a bank, up to a set amount.
It sets the interest rate on every loan.
It lends money to the states.

questions.feedback_correct: Congress created it in 1933, after thousands of banks failed in the Great Depression.

quizzes.title: 7.4 Critical Questions: Hamilton, Report on Public Credit
quizzes.description: Two questions on Hamilton’s argument for paying the debt. Read the source first.

questions.text: Hamilton writes that “The faith of America has been repeatedly pledged” for the debt. What is he arguing?

answers.text: The debt is too large to be repaid.
Other nations will pay the debt for America.
The nation has promised again and again to pay, so refusing would break its word.
Only the states made promises to lenders.

questions.feedback_correct: To pledge faith is to give a promise. Hamilton treats the debt as a promise the nation must keep.

questions.text: Hamilton says that a nation which does not keep its engagements will still be respected and trusted.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: He says that the “reverse” is the fate of those who break their engagements.

quizzes.title: 7.7 Reading Quiz: Taxes, the Whiskey Rebellion, and Public Services
quizzes.description: Five questions on the kinds of taxes, the Whiskey Rebellion, and what citizens expect from government.

questions.text: Why did the tax on whiskey fall so hard on farmers on the western frontier?

answers.text: Whiskey was against the law in the West.
Western farmers did not grow any grain.
Grain was costly to haul over the mountains, and turning it into whiskey was how many farmers reached a market.
Tax collectors lived only in the West.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson says the tax fell on the one product that let a frontier farmer reach a market.

questions.text: Which choice best describes how President Washington answered the rebellion?

answers.text: He ordered the rebels home, sent commissioners to talk, called up a militia army, and later pardoned the two men convicted of treason.
He ignored the protest until it ended.
He repealed the tax at once to calm the farmers.
He punished every protester with the full penalty for treason.

questions.feedback_correct: Washington used force first and mercy after.

questions.text: Which level of government depends mostly on property taxes?

answers.text: The national government.
The Supreme Court.
The state legislature.
Local governments, which use them for schools, police, and fire protection.

questions.feedback_correct: The national government relies mostly on income and payroll taxes, and states rely on sales taxes.

questions.text: What did the 16th Amendment do?

answers.text: It forbade the nation to tax incomes.
It let Congress tax incomes, which grew into the main source of money for the national government.
It created the sales tax.
It gave the states power to tax goods from other countries.

questions.feedback_correct: The states ratified it in 1913.

questions.text: The lesson says that citizens in a republic have a better road than armed protest. What is it?

answers.text: Petition Congress, write to newspapers, and vote against the lawmakers who passed the law.
Refuse to pay and gather arms.
Wait for the President to pardon everyone.
Move to another state.

questions.feedback_correct: Many western farmers did just that, and they helped to elect Jefferson.

quizzes.title: 7.8 Critical Questions: Washington, Proclamation on the Whiskey Rebellion
quizzes.description: Two questions on what the President said to the western counties and what he ordered. Read the source first.

questions.text: What reason does Washington give for needing more than the ordinary courts?

answers.text: There were no courts in western Pennsylvania.
The laws had been opposed by combinations too powerful to be suppressed by the ordinary course of judicial proceedings.
The judges had refused to hear the cases.
The protesters had already been found innocent.

questions.feedback_correct: The text says that ordinary judicial proceedings could not suppress the opposition.

questions.text: Which two things does Washington command the insurgents to do?

answers.text: To disperse
To retire peaceably to their homes
To hand over their land to the government
To pay the tax in gold

questions.feedback_correct: The text commands them to “disperse and retire peaceably to their respective abodes.”

quizzes.title: 7.12 Reading Quiz: Smith, Hamilton, and the Mixed Economy
quizzes.description: Five questions on how a market economy works, how it differs from a command economy, and what a mixed economy is.

questions.text: After a hurricane, the price of plywood in Florida rises. What does the higher price do?

answers.text: It stops builders from buying anything.
It tells the government to take over the lumber business.
It makes sellers close their shops.
It tells sellers in other states that plywood is wanted here, so they send more.

questions.feedback_correct: The price carried the message, and thousands of sellers answered it.

questions.text: What did Smith say that a market needs from the law?

answers.text: Nothing. A market runs best with no rules at all.
Courts that enforce contracts, laws that keep people honest, and safe property.
A law that sets the price of every good.
A rule that only rich people may trade.

questions.feedback_correct: A market needs rule of law, just as a republic does.

questions.text: How did Jefferson and Hamilton differ in what they hoped for the republic?

answers.text: Jefferson wanted factories, and Hamilton wanted farms.
Both wanted a command economy.
Jefferson thought the best citizens were independent farmers, and Hamilton argued that manufacturing would make the country stronger.
Both wanted the nation to stop trading with other countries.

questions.feedback_correct: Both men were thinking like classical republicans, but they answered the question differently.

questions.text: Why is the Erie Canal an example of a mixed economy?

answers.text: The government of New York paid for it, and private farmers and merchants used it to ship and sell goods.
The national government took over all shipping.
A private company built it with no help from any government.
It ended trade between the Midwest and the East.

questions.feedback_correct: In a mixed economy, private people make most decisions but government also plays a part.

questions.text: Who gained and who paid because of the early tariffs?

answers.text: Everyone gained equally.
Only farmers gained.
Tariffs ended in 1800, so no one was affected.
American makers of cloth, iron, and tools gained, and a farmer who bought tools paid more.

questions.feedback_correct: Americans argued about who should gain and who should pay, and that argument is part of life in a mixed economy.

quizzes.title: 7.14 Critical Questions: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations
quizzes.description: Two questions on Smith’s famous “invisible hand.” Read the source first.

questions.text: In this passage, Smith says that the merchant sets out to help society.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: Smith says the merchant “intends only his own gain” and is led by an invisible hand to help others.

questions.text: Smith writes that by pursuing his own interest a person “frequently” promotes the interest of society. What does the word “frequently” tell you?

answers.text: Self-interest always helps society.
Self-interest often helps society, but Smith does not claim that it always does.
Self-interest never helps society.
Self-interest helps only the rich.

questions.feedback_correct: A careful reader notices that Smith says “frequently,” not “always.”

quizzes.title: 7.18 Critical Questions: The Sherman Antitrust Act
quizzes.description: Two questions on the text of the nation’s first antitrust law. Read the source first.

questions.text: Section 2 punishes a person who “shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize.” What do the words “attempt to” add?

answers.text: Only people who succeed in taking over a market are punished.
Only companies, and not persons, can be punished.
Trying and failing to take over a market is legal.
A person can be guilty even if the attempt to take over a market did not succeed.

questions.feedback_correct: The law reaches the attempt as well as the success.

questions.text: Which two punishments does Section 2 allow?

answers.text: A fine not exceeding five thousand dollars
Imprisonment of up to ten years
Imprisonment not exceeding one year
Loss of citizenship

questions.feedback_correct: The text also allows both punishments together, at the court’s discretion.

quizzes.title: 7.22 Reading Quiz: Planned Economies: The Soviet Union and China
quizzes.description: Five questions on the promises of the Communist Manifesto and what happened in the Soviet Union and China.

questions.text: Which of these did The Communist Manifesto promise?

answers.text: A society with no classes and no need for a government to rule over anyone.
A free market with no rules.
A king chosen by the workers.
A government that would grow larger forever.

questions.feedback_correct: The leaders who followed Marx did not make the government fade away. They made it all-powerful.

questions.text: Why did a planned economy do so badly at making ordinary goods?

answers.text: The Soviet Union had no factories.
Workers refused to work.
The planners set the prices, so prices could not tell them what people wanted, and shortages and waste followed.
Citizens wanted very few goods.

questions.feedback_correct: A planner in a distant office had to guess how many shoes and shoelaces a hundred million people needed.

questions.text: Why did the famine of the Great Leap Forward become so deadly?

answers.text: Bad weather alone caused it.
Officials were afraid to report bad news, so they reported harvests that did not exist, and the state took grain based on the false numbers.
Other countries refused to sell China food.
Mao banned farming.

questions.feedback_correct: A free press or an election might have let the truth out sooner.

questions.text: What was collectivization?

answers.text: Letting farmers buy more land.
Giving farmers new machines.
Ending all taxes on farms.
Forcing farmers to give up their land, animals, and tools and join large state-run farms.

questions.feedback_correct: It led to resistance and then to the famine of 1932 and 1933.

questions.text: What do China’s reforms after Mao show?

answers.text: That markets always fail.
That markets bring freedom automatically.
That incomes rose when markets were allowed, but China did not become a free republic.
That command economies work better than markets.

questions.feedback_correct: A market can be added without freedom following.

quizzes.title: 7.24 Critical Questions: Marx and Engels, The Communist Manifesto
quizzes.description: Two questions on what the Manifesto said its followers wanted. Read the source first.

questions.text: The authors say that the theory of the Communists may be summed up in a single sentence. What is it?

answers.text: Free trade in all goods.
Abolition of private property.
Rule by a king.
Lower taxes for everyone.

questions.feedback_correct: This is the idea that led to command economies.

questions.text: Which two measures from the list put economic power in the hands of the government?

answers.text: Abolition of property in land and use of all rents for public purposes
Free choice of jobs for every worker
Centralization of credit in the hands of the State
Competition among private banks

questions.feedback_correct: Both steps move land or lending out of private hands and into the government’s.

quizzes.title: 7.27 Reading Quiz: Measuring Standard of Living: GDP Per Capita
quizzes.description: Five questions on how GDP per capita measures a standard of living and what it shows about different economic systems.

questions.text: Why do economists divide GDP by the number of people?

answers.text: To make large countries look larger.
A large country can have a large GDP and still be poor, and a per-person number compares countries fairly.
To count only the people who work.
To remove the effect of taxes.

questions.feedback_correct: Think of the party with a hundred guests and the party with ten.

questions.text: Which of these does GDP per capita not show?

answers.text: The total value of what a country makes in a year.
The average amount produced per person.
The value of what a country makes and sells.
How wealth is shared, how much unpaid work is done, or whether people are free to speak and vote.

questions.feedback_correct: It is a useful tool, but it is only one tool.

questions.text: Why do the divisions of Germany and Korea work like experiments?

answers.text: The people on each side shared a language, history, and culture, so the main thing that changed was the system.
The two sides spoke different languages.
Both sides chose the same system.
Neither side kept any records.

questions.feedback_correct: In both cases the market half grew far richer than the command half.

questions.text: Which of these is one of the reasons economists give for why markets do better?

answers.text: Governments set every price.
Planners know what everyone wants.
People who may keep the reward for hard work or a good idea work harder and try more things.
The state owns all property.

questions.feedback_correct: The other reasons are prices, property, and the rule of law.

questions.text: Which of these can a market not do alone?

answers.text: Let sellers compete for customers.
Let people choose their jobs.
Let prices change when goods become scarce.
Protect itself from monopolies, or provide national defense, or give every family a fair start.

questions.feedback_correct: Citizens of a republic have to decide how far government should go. A mixed economy is the American way of answering.

quizzes.title: 7.28 Critical Questions: Reagan, Address at the Brandenburg Gate

quizzes.title: Module 8 Intro: A Republic Tested
quizzes.description:
In this module you will study a republic that was given away from the inside, and a republic that was struck from the outside. You will ask how a free people can lose its freedoms one step at a time, and how it can defend itself without giving up what it is defending. These questions come first so that you can see how your answers change by the end.

By the end of this module you will be able to:

  • describe how the Nazi government took away German Jews’ citizenship and carried out the Holocaust;
  • describe the attacks of September 11 and the steps the nation took in response;
  • explain how safety and liberty can pull against each other, using Korematsu v. United States as an earlier test.

quizzes.title: 8.2 Reading Quiz: From Weimar to the Holocaust
quizzes.description: Five questions on how the Weimar Republic ended and how the Nazi government carried out the Holocaust.

questions.text: What made many Germans lose trust in the Weimar Republic?

answers.text: It had no constitution.
It never held an election.
Many blamed it for the defeat and the Treaty of Versailles, and then hyperinflation and the Depression left millions without savings or work.
The Kaiser returned to power.

questions.feedback_correct: Frightened people looked for someone to blame, and for someone to save them.

questions.text: How did Hitler become chancellor?

answers.text: President Hindenburg named him in January 1933 after conservative politicians urged it, thinking they could use the Nazis and keep control.
The Nazis won a majority of the votes.
The army seized the parliament building.
Every German voted for him directly.

questions.feedback_correct: The Nazis did not have a majority, and their vote had just slipped. It did not have to happen.

questions.text: What did the Enabling Act do?

answers.text: It gave voters the right to remove the chancellor.
It let the chancellor and his cabinet make laws without the parliament for four years.
It ended the Treaty of Versailles.
It made Hindenburg emperor.

questions.feedback_correct: It passed with two thirds of the vote, because many who would have voted no were in jail or hiding.

questions.text: What did the Nuremberg Laws do to German Jews?

answers.text: They gave Jews full citizenship.
They required Jews to serve in the army.
They moved Jews to a separate country.
They made Jews subjects with no political rights, because only people of “German blood” could be citizens.

questions.feedback_correct: A government took the power to decide who its people are and used it to strip a whole group of citizenship.

questions.text: What principle did the Nuremberg trials set down?

answers.text: Following orders is no excuse for committing crimes against humanity.
Only soldiers can be tried for war crimes.
Trials of this kind must be held in secret.
Only the winners of a war can hold trials.

questions.feedback_correct: The judges heard the evidence in open court, the opposite of how the Nazi state had worked.

questions.text: Article 2 says that only a subject “of German or kindred blood” can be a citizen. What does this rule do?

answers.text: It makes citizenship depend on ancestry, not only on what a person does.
It gives citizenship to everyone born in Germany.
It requires every citizen to take an oath.
It lets the parliament vote on each person.

questions.feedback_correct: A person cannot change his ancestors, so no good conduct could earn citizenship.

questions.text: Under the text, a subject of the State who is not a citizen still has full political rights.

answers.text: True
False

Every government in the Arab world is an enemy of America.

questions.text: Bush says that “our first responsibility is to live by” America’s principles. What does he mean?

Principles matter less than safety.
Only the government has to follow the principles.
