quizzes.title: 8.11 Quarter 3 Exam: The Republic’s Upkeep
quizzes.description: Forty multiple-choice questions on this quarter’s work: citizens and the vote, the watchful citizen, the republic at home, money and markets, and how a republic is tested. Work alone and without notes. You have one attempt.

questions.text: What did the 14th Amendment say about who is a citizen?

answers.text: Only free people of European ancestry may become citizens of the United States, whether by birth or by oath.
A person is a citizen only if the state where he or she lives has first voted to grant citizenship.
Anyone born or naturalized in the United States and under its laws is a citizen, whatever the person’s race.
Only children of citizens count, so immigrants and their children must wait for Congress to act.

questions.text: Wong Kim Ark was born in San Francisco to Chinese parents, and officials refused to let him come home from a trip abroad. What did the Supreme Court decide?

answers.text: He was not a citizen, because the law barred his parents from becoming citizens themselves.
His birth on American soil made him a citizen, even though his parents could not be naturalized.
He could return only if Congress passed a special law that admitted him by name to the country.
He was a citizen only if he took an oath in court after reaching the age of twenty-one.

questions.text: Which of these is a responsibility that a free citizen chooses, rather than an obligation the law requires?

answers.text: Paying income taxes each year.
Serving on a jury when summoned.
Obeying the traffic laws of the state.
Volunteering to help in the community.

questions.text: Why did Washington say that a free people needs virtue?

answers.text: A virtuous people can run a government without paying any taxes to support its courts or army.
Laws can force a duty but cannot make a person care, and a people without self-control will need a strong ruler.
Virtue replaces elections, so a people who have it need not choose their own leaders by vote.
A people with enough virtue needs no written laws, since each person will always do what is right.

questions.text: People born in American Samoa are U.S. nationals but not automatically citizens. What does this show?

answers.text: The 14th Amendment was repealed, and Congress now grants citizenship only through a yearly lottery.
Birth in any territory of the United States always makes a person a full citizen at once.
Citizenship is set by Congress and the courts, and it can differ for people in territories.
Each territory’s governor decides on his own who counts as a citizen of the United States.

questions.text: Which steps does Article V require to amend the Constitution?

answers.text: A majority of Congress proposes the amendment, and the President signs it into law.
A majority of the states propose the amendment, and the Supreme Court gives its approval.
The President proposes the amendment, and two thirds of the Senate gives its consent.
Two thirds of Congress propose the amendment, and three fourths of the states ratify it.

questions.text: After the 15th Amendment was ratified, how did Southern states work around it?

answers.text: They passed state laws that openly repealed the 15th Amendment within their own borders.
They used poll taxes and literacy tests that did not name race but were applied unfairly.
They asked the Supreme Court to declare the amendment void soon after it was ratified.
They stopped holding elections and let the governors name every officeholder.

questions.text: Why did the writers of the Declaration of Sentiments copy the form of the Declaration of Independence?

answers.text: To ask the British king to take the American colonies back into the empire.
To claim that women alone should hold the offices of the national government.
To show that the American promise of liberty was meant for women too.
To win a lawsuit that was then pending before the Supreme Court.

questions.text: What happened in the Tennessee House in August 1920?

answers.text: The House rejected the 19th Amendment by a single vote, and the amendment then failed for a decade.
A young member changed his vote to yes, and Tennessee ratified the 19th Amendment by 49 to 47.
The Governor vetoed the 19th Amendment, and the House could not muster votes to override him.
The House passed the 15th Amendment after a long debate over the vote for women.

questions.text: Under the Elections Clause, who mainly decides how elections for Congress are run?

answers.text: The states, though Congress may change the rules.
The President, though the Senate may change the rules.
The Supreme Court, though the states may change the rules.
The Electoral College, though the House may change the rules.

questions.text: The House has been fixed at 435 seats since 1929. What may happen to a state whose population grows more slowly than the nation’s?

answers.text: It may lose seats after a census, since a seat gained by one state must be lost by another.
It gains seats after a census, because the House must grow to match the nation’s population.
It keeps the same seats forever, since the Constitution fixes each state’s number of seats.
It must hold a special election, since every seat in the House is then up for a new vote.

questions.text: Which problem in the election of 1800 did the 12th Amendment fix?

answers.text: Electors had no separate vote for Vice President, so two candidates of one party could tie.
Electors were chosen by the Senate, so the people had no say in who the electors would be.
The President was elected for life, so no election could ever change who held the office.
Only the House could count the electoral votes, so a tie could never be settled at all.

questions.text: Why did Hamilton urge fellow Federalists to choose Jefferson over Burr in 1801?

answers.text: He had been promised a high office by Jefferson if the House voted for him on a certain ballot.
He wanted Burr to take power as a strong ruler, since Burr shared his views on the economy.
He hoped the House would fail to choose, so that the Federalists could name a new President by law.
He disliked Jefferson but distrusted Burr more, and judged Jefferson a man of principle.

questions.text: Why does the lesson stress that power passed from one party to another in 1800 without soldiers?

answers.text: It proved that the Electoral College is a perfect system that never needs repair or change.
It showed that John Adams had really won the election, though the House gave it to Jefferson.
It showed that a republic can survive a bitter election when the losers accept the result.
It ended political parties in America for a generation, because both sides then agreed on policy.

questions.text: Why was the jury’s verdict in the Zenger trial a surprise?

answers.text: Under the old rule, the jury was only to decide whether Zenger printed the words, and he had.
Zenger had refused to attend his own trial, and the jury had to decide the case without him.
The governor had chosen the jurors himself, and everyone expected them to side with him.
The judge had told the jury that the printed words were true and that Zenger must go free.

questions.text: Which statement is true of the burden of proof in a criminal trial?

answers.text: The government must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and the accused need not prove innocence.
The accused must prove his or her innocence to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt at every trial.
The judge alone decides what must be proved, and the jury only repeats the judge’s conclusion.
The jury must gather the evidence itself, since neither side may bring any witnesses to court.

questions.text: How was the Sedition Act of 1798 mostly used?

answers.text: Against foreign soldiers who had landed on the coast during the undeclared war with France.
Against Federalist printers who had published attacks on the new Vice President.
Against Republican editors and writers who criticized the Federalist government.
Against citizens who had refused to pay the new taxes that the Federalists had passed.

questions.text: Which set of questions best helps a citizen judge a source for bias?

answers.text: How long is it, how old is it, and in what city was it printed?
Who made it, who was it made for, and what does it want me to do?
How many people have read it, how much did it cost, and who owns the press?
Is it signed, is it dated, and is it printed in more than one color of ink?

questions.text: A person wins a court judgment in Georgia and wants to collect in Florida. Which rule in Article IV makes Florida respect the judgment?

answers.text: Privileges and immunities.
The Supremacy Clause.
Judicial review.
Full faith and credit.

questions.text: Madison wrote that the powers of the national government are “few and defined” and those of the states “numerous and indefinite.” What did he mean?

answers.text: The nation handles a short list of large tasks, and the states handle most of daily life.
The states may ignore any national law that they find to be unwise or too costly to carry out.
The nation has only a few powers, so it must ask the states for every dollar it spends.
The states handle only a few tasks, so the nation must run the schools and local police.

questions.text: Which statement shows a way that Florida’s constitution differs from the national Constitution?

answers.text: It ends with a Declaration of Rights and is harder to change.
It has no courts and gives all judging to the Governor.
It begins with a Declaration of Rights and is easier to change.
It overrules the national Constitution when the two conflict.

questions.text: A state agency writes detailed rules saying how often restaurant kitchens must be inspected. Which source of law is this?

answers.text: A regulation.
A constitution.
A statute.
A precedent.

questions.text: Residents of a Florida town want pumps to stop their streets from flooding. After researching the problem, what is the next step in the lesson’s method?

answers.text: Find the agency in charge, such as the city’s public works department.
Write to the President, who holds the final say over every local street in the country.
Wait for the state legislature to notice the problem and pass a law about it on its own.
Choose a course of action first, and learn later which office has the power to carry it out.

questions.text: How did Jefferson and Hamilton disagree about the national bank?

answers.text: Jefferson wanted a larger national bank than Hamilton did, and Hamilton wanted the states to run it.
Both said the states should charter a bank, but they quarreled over how many banks to allow.
Hamilton said the Bill of Rights forbade a bank, and Jefferson said the Preamble required one.
Jefferson said the Constitution gave Congress no power to charter a bank, and Hamilton said the “necessary and proper” power covered it.

questions.text: Why did the whiskey excise tax fall so hard on western farmers?

answers.text: They were the only people in the country who bought whiskey, so they paid the whole of the tax.
Whiskey was how they carried value over the mountains to market, so the tax hit their main way to earn money.
The tax applied only to farms west of the mountains, and easterners were free of it altogether.
Western farmers had to pay the tax twice, once to the state and again to the national government.

questions.text: How did Washington answer the Whiskey Rebellion?

answers.text: He repealed the tax at once and sent a letter of apology to every farmer in the western counties.
He ignored the protest until it died away, and no one was ever arrested or tried for it.
He asked Britain to send soldiers, and he refused to forgive any of the rebels who were caught.
He sent a militia army to enforce the law and later pardoned the two men convicted of treason.

questions.text: Which amendment lets Congress tax incomes?

answers.text: The 12th Amendment.
The 14th Amendment.
The 24th Amendment.
The 16th Amendment.

questions.text: In a market economy, what does a rising price tell producers?

answers.text: The government has set a new price, and they must obey it from now on without question.
The good is scarce or wanted, and they should make more of it.
The good is no longer wanted, and they should stop making it as quickly as they can.
The market has failed, and officials must now take over the making of the good themselves.

questions.text: Why is the Erie Canal an example of a mixed economy?

answers.text: A single private company built it, and no government had any part in its cost or its use.
The national government set every price on it, and private traders were barred from using it.
The state of New York paid for it, and private farmers and merchants used it to trade.
It was built to replace all private trade, and farmers had to hand their goods to the state.

questions.text: What did the Sherman Antitrust Act make a crime?

answers.text: Joining together to restrain trade, and monopolizing a market.
Owning a business that employed more than a hundred workers in any one state.
Charging a price for a good that was higher than the cost of making it.
Selling goods across state lines without first paying a fee to the national government.

questions.text: Beyond prices, why did a republic worry about giant monopolies?

answers.text: Monopolies always paid their workers less than the law allowed, and the courts could not stop it.
The Constitution said in plain words that no business could grow past a certain size.
Wealth gathered in a few hands can become political power, so ordinary citizens lose their say.
Monopolies kept the census from being taken, because they would not let counters in their factories.

questions.text: Why did planned economies, such as that of the Soviet Union, produce so many shortages?

answers.text: Too many private businesses competed with one another, and they wasted goods on needless variety.
Prices rose and fell too freely, so planners could never tell what a good was worth to buyers.
Citizens were free to choose their own jobs, and too many of them chose to leave the factories.
Officials set the prices and goals, so planners lacked honest signals about what people wanted.

questions.text: Why did the famine in China from 1958 to 1962 grow worse?

answers.text: Farmers refused to plant crops, because the government had offered them higher pay for staying home.
Private farms hoarded grain for sale on a black market, and the state could not find it.
Foreign countries stopped all trade with China, and no grain could be brought in from abroad.
Local officials feared to report bad news and reported harvests that did not exist, so the state took grain on false numbers.

questions.text: What do China’s market reforms after 1978 show?

answers.text: Markets raised incomes, but they did not by themselves make China a free republic.
Markets always lead to a free vote, so China became a republic once its economy had grown.
Command economies always grow faster than markets, so the reforms were abandoned in time.
Incomes did not change after the reforms, so China stayed as poor as it had been under Mao.

questions.text: Why do economists divide GDP by the number of people?

answers.text: To count how many people in the country have jobs and how many of them are looking for work.
To compare how much each person gets, since a large country can have a large GDP and still be poor.
To prove that large countries are always richer than small countries in goods and services.
To remove the effect of prices, so that every country’s output is measured in the same money.

questions.text: Why are West and East Germany a good “natural experiment”?

answers.text: The two sides were made up of very different peoples, so any gap in wealth was no surprise.
The people shared a language and history but chose different systems and got different results.
Both sides chose command economies, and the only difference between them was their size.
Neither side kept any records, so later economists could compare them only by guesswork.

questions.text: Why does the lesson say the Nazi rise to power “did not have to happen”?

answers.text: The Nazis had won every election since 1919, and Hindenburg had no choice but to obey the voters.
Germany had no constitution, so no one could say who had the right to name a chancellor.
The Nazis had no majority and their vote had slipped, and Hindenburg could have chosen otherwise.
The army had already taken the government, so Hindenburg’s choice made no difference at all.

questions.text: What is genocide?

answers.text: A war fought between two neighboring countries.
The removal of a government by a free election.
A law that limits trade between nations.
The deliberate killing of a whole people or group.

questions.text: Which actions did the nation take after the attacks of September 11?

answers.text: Congress ended all immigration, closed the federal courts, and put the President in charge of every state.
Congress authorized force against those who planned the attacks, passed the Patriot Act, and created the Department of Homeland Security.
The states amended the Constitution to give the President a third term and then left the United Nations.
The nation withdrew its armed forces from the world and signed a treaty of peace with the attackers.

questions.text: What did the Supreme Court decide in Korematsu v. United States (1944), and how is it viewed now?

answers.text: It struck down the order, and the army obeyed, so no Japanese Americans were ever sent to camps.
It ruled that the President has no emergency powers, and the ruling still stands without question.
It upheld the order removing Japanese Americans from the West Coast, and the decision is now widely seen as wrong.
It upheld the order, and later courts and Congress have always agreed that the decision was right.

quizzes.title: Module 9 Intro: Origins
quizzes.description:
In this module you will go back to the roots of the American republic. You will ask what ideas the Founders took from Athens, Rome, and Jerusalem and from English charters, how the Enlightenment and the quarrel with Britain led to the Declaration, and how the Constitution was written and won approval.   • describe the British policies that led to the Declaration and match its grievances to the rights it says were violated;
  • explain the failures of the Articles of Confederation, how the Constitution answered each one, and why the Federalists and Anti-Federalists argued over a bill of rights.

quizzes.title: 9.2 Reading Quiz: Greece, Rome, and Jerusalem
quizzes.description: Five questions on what the Founders took from Athens, Rome, and the Judeo-Christian tradition, and how each had failed before.

questions.text: What happened in Athens in 404 BC, and what does the lesson take from it?

answers.text: The Athenians gave up voting forever, which shows that democracy cannot work.
A king was crowned, which shows that Athens wanted a ruler.
A small group of rich men took control and ruled by fear, but the citizens drove them out within a year, which shows that free government can be lost and won back.
Sparta joined Athens, which shows that city-states are stronger together.

questions.feedback_correct: The lesson cuts two ways: free government can be lost in a bad year, and people willing to fight for it can win it back.

questions.text: How was Roman government different from Athenian government?

answers.text: Roman citizens elected officials to act for them, and did not vote on every law themselves.
Roman citizens never voted at all.
Roman government was ruled by one king for its whole history.
Roman citizens voted directly on every law in a great Assembly.

questions.feedback_correct: This is representative government: citizens choose people to act in their name.

questions.text: Why did the Romans write the laws on the Twelve Tables and set them up in the public square?

answers.text: So that the nobles could change the laws more easily.
So that only judges could read the laws.
So that a king could be crowned.
So that anyone, rich or poor, could read what the law said, and judges could not bend it.

questions.feedback_correct: This is the rule of law: laws that are known in advance and that bind everyone, including those who make them.

questions.text: According to Polybius, why did Rome grow so strong?

answers.text: It had the largest army in the world.
It mixed three kinds of government, a king-like consul, an aristocratic Senate, and democratic assemblies, so each part held back the other two.
It chose its leaders by lot.
It had no written laws to slow it down.

questions.feedback_correct: This mixed constitution points toward the separation of powers.

questions.text: What does the story of King David and the prophet Nathan teach?

answers.text: A king may do as he pleases if he is wise.
A prophet should never speak to a king.
Even the most powerful ruler must answer to a law higher than his own wishes.
Only the wealthy have to obey the law.

questions.feedback_correct: The Founders used this idea against King George, and in the Constitution against any ruler.

quizzes.title: 9.4 Critical Questions: Magna Carta (1215)
quizzes.description: Two questions on a clause of the Great Charter. Read the source first.

questions.text: A clause of the charter says that no free man shall be seized or imprisoned or stripped of his possessions “except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.” What must the king do before he punishes a free man?

answers.text: Follow the law and a lawful judgment first.
Ask the Pope for permission.
Pay the man for his property.
Give the man a place in Parliament.

questions.feedback_correct: This is the root of due process.

questions.text: Under this clause, the protection applies to every person in England, including those who were not free.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: The text names the “free man.” Many people in 1215 were not free, and the protection did not reach them. Later generations widened it.

quizzes.title: 9.7 Reading Quiz: Magna Carta to Paine
quizzes.description: Five questions on four steps on the road from medieval England to the American Revolution.

questions.text: Which American idea began with the clause in Magna Carta that a king must follow the law before he punishes a free man?

answers.text: Judicial review.
Due process.
The Electoral College.
The Necessary and Proper Clause.

questions.feedback_correct: The Fifth Amendment says that no person may be deprived of life, liberty, or property “without due process of law.”

questions.text: What happened to Magna Carta soon after King John sealed it?

answers.text: The Pope declared it annulled, and civil war followed. Later it was reissued and confirmed again and again.
It was copied at once into the laws of France.
Every baron signed it, and peace followed.
John kept every promise he had made.

questions.feedback_correct: It was a fragile victory, and it became the foundation of English liberty only because later kings confirmed it.

questions.text: Why is the Mayflower Compact an early example of government by consent?

answers.text: A king wrote it for the colony.
It set up a Parliament.
The passengers made their own government by agreeing together, and no king gave it to them.
It was signed by every person in England.

questions.feedback_correct: The same idea echoes in the opening words of the Constitution: “We the People.”

questions.text: Which American clause echoes the English Bill of Rights ban on “cruel and unusual” punishments?

answers.text: The First Amendment.
The Preamble.
The Tenth Amendment.
The Eighth Amendment.

questions.feedback_correct: Americans copied those words from the English Bill of Rights of 1689.

questions.text: What did Thomas Paine’s pamphlet Common Sense argue?

answers.text: That the colonies should keep trying to reconcile with the king.
That a king was no better than any other man, and that America should govern itself.
That Parliament should tax the colonies more.
That the colonies should join France.

questions.feedback_correct: It helped turn a quarrel over taxes into a movement for independence.

quizzes.title: 9.8 Critical Questions: The Mayflower Compact (1620)
quizzes.description: Two questions on the agreement the Pilgrims signed aboard their ship. Read the source first.

questions.text: The signers promise to “combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politic.” What are they doing?

answers.text: Asking the king to choose their leaders.
Forming a government by their own agreement.
Planning to return to England.
Dividing the land among themselves.

questions.feedback_correct: No king gave them this government. They made it themselves.

questions.text: Which two statements does the Compact make or imply about the signers? Select two.

answers.text: They will make “just and equal Laws” for the good of the colony.
They promise “due submission and obedience” to the laws they set up.
The king will appoint every officer.
Each person may ignore any law he dislikes.

questions.feedback_correct: Notice that they bind themselves to laws that they make together. That is consent.

quizzes.title: 9.12 Reading Quiz: The Enlightenment and Natural Rights
quizzes.description: Five questions on four Enlightenment thinkers, natural rights, the social contract, and how the Declaration uses them.

questions.text: Why did Thomas Hobbes say that people give up some freedom to a strong ruler?

answers.text: Because rulers are always wise.
Because without any government, everyone would fight everyone else and life would be “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.”
Because natural rights come from the ruler.
Because the people had voted for a king.

questions.feedback_correct: Hobbes wanted a ruler with almost unlimited power. Most Americans thought this went too far, but they agreed that government exists because people need protection.

questions.text: What did John Locke say about natural rights?

answers.text: They are given by the government and may be taken back.
They belong only to the rich.
Every person is born with rights to life, liberty, and property, and government exists to protect them.
They are found only in Rome.

questions.feedback_correct: Since people form a government by agreement, it has only the power that they give it. That is consent of the governed.

questions.text: Congress makes the laws, the President carries them out, and the courts judge cases. Which idea does this describe?

answers.text: Checks and balances.
The social contract.
The right of revolution.
Separation of powers.

questions.feedback_correct: Separation of powers divides the jobs. Checks and balances lets each branch limit the others.

questions.text: Which of these is an example of checks and balances, not of separation of powers?

answers.text: Congress passes a bill.
A judge hears a case.
The President vetoes a bill that Congress passed.
The Senate meets in its own chamber.

questions.feedback_correct: A veto is one branch limiting another.

questions.text: Which idea did Rousseau add to the discussion?

answers.text: A government is only fair when it rests on the shared will of the whole people.
Government should be run by a hereditary king.
Three branches should divide the power.
Life is safer without any laws.

questions.feedback_correct: Americans borrowed Rousseau’s belief that the people are the source of government power, but they mostly built on Locke and Montesquieu.

quizzes.title: 9.14 Critical Questions: The English Bill of Rights (1689)
quizzes.description: Two questions on what Parliament required of the Crown after the Glorious Revolution. Read the source first.

questions.text: The text says that raising or keeping a standing army in time of peace, unless it is with the consent of Parliament, is against law. What does this limit?

answers.text: The right of the people to petition.
The king’s power to keep an army in peacetime without Parliament’s consent.
The power of the courts to hold trials.
The size of Parliament.

questions.feedback_correct: Compare this with the Declaration of Independence, which charges the king with keeping “Standing Armies among us, in times of peace.”

questions.text: Under the text, the king may collect money for the Crown on his own authority, without a grant from Parliament.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: The text says that levying money for the Crown without a grant of Parliament is illegal.

quizzes.title: 9.18 Critical Questions: The Declaration of Independence
quizzes.description: Two questions on the principles and the charges in the Declaration. Read the source first.

questions.text: The Declaration says that governments derive “their just powers from the consent of the governed.” What does this say about where a government gets its power?

answers.text: From a king chosen by God alone.
From the strongest army.
From the people it governs.
From the oldest family.

questions.feedback_correct: This is Locke’s idea of consent.

questions.text: Which two of these are among the charges the Declaration makes against King George? Select two.

answers.text: He imposed “Taxes on us without our Consent.”
He deprived colonists, in many cases, “of the benefits of Trial by Jury.”
He closed every church in the colonies.
He forbade colonists to print newspapers.

questions.feedback_correct: Each charge says that the king did something and that it violated a right. Match the charge to the right.

quizzes.title: 9.22 Reading Quiz: The Articles of Confederation to the Constitution
quizzes.description: Five questions on the weaknesses of the Articles, Shays’ Rebellion, the Philadelphia Convention, and how the Constitution answered each failure.

questions.text: Why could Congress under the Articles not pay the soldiers who had won the war?

answers.text: There were no soldiers to pay.
The President refused to sign the bills.
The states had agreed to pay them directly.
Congress could not tax. It could only ask the states for money, and they often did not send it.

questions.feedback_correct: Money was the first weakness of the Articles.

questions.text: Why were the Articles almost impossible to change?

answers.text: An amendment needed all thirteen states to agree, so one state could block it.
Only the President could propose changes.
The Supreme Court had to approve every change.
They could be changed only once a century.

questions.feedback_correct: Article V of the Constitution lets three fourths of the states approve an amendment.

questions.text: What did Shays’ Rebellion show?

answers.text: That farmers were pleased with their taxes.
That Massachusetts had no courts.
That the Articles worked well.
That a government without money or an army could not keep order, and leaders feared people would turn to a strong man.

questions.feedback_correct: The old story of Athens and Rome seemed to be repeating.

questions.text: How did the Great Compromise settle the quarrel between large and small states?

answers.text: Every state got one vote in a single house.
Seats in the House go by population, and each state has two senators.
Only the large states would send delegates.
Congress would be dropped and the President would rule.

questions.feedback_correct: Congress would have two houses. This saved the convention.

questions.text: The Preamble says “establish Justice.” Which failure of the Articles does this answer?

answers.text: The states taxed one another’s goods.
Congress could not raise an army.
There were no national courts to settle disputes.
The Articles could not be amended.

questions.feedback_correct: Article III created a Supreme Court and let Congress set up lower ones.

quizzes.title: 9.24 Critical Questions: The Articles of Confederation
quizzes.description: Two questions on how the first American government divided power. Read the source first.

questions.text: Article II says that each state keeps “every power, jurisdiction, and right” that is not “expressly delegated” to Congress. What does this show about the Articles?

answers.text: The central government held nearly all the power.
The states kept most of the power, and Congress had only what the states gave it.
The states had no power at all.
The President held most of the power.

questions.feedback_correct: This is a confederation. Compare how the Constitution divides power.

questions.text: Under Article XIII, a change to the Articles must be confirmed by the legislatures of every state.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: One state could therefore block any change. Compare the three-fourths rule in Article V of the Constitution.

quizzes.title: 9.27 Reading Quiz: Ratification, Rule of Law, and Sources of Law
quizzes.description: Five questions on the ratification debate, the Bill of Rights, the rule of law, and the main sources and types of law.

questions.text: What was the main worry of the Anti-Federalists?

answers.text: That the Constitution gave too much power to the states.
That a national government far from home would become a tyranny, and that the Constitution had no list of rights.
That Congress would have only one house.
That the President would have no power.

questions.feedback_correct: Federalists answered that a government with only listed powers could not violate rights it had no power to touch.

questions.text: What finally carried the day in Virginia and New York?

answers.text: The Federalists took back the Constitution.
Every Anti-Federalist changed sides.
A promise that the first Congress would take up a bill of rights.
A new vote of the whole country.

questions.feedback_correct: The votes were very close, 89 to 79 in Virginia and 30 to 27 in New York.

questions.text: How many of the twelve amendments Congress sent to the states became the Bill of Rights by 1791?

answers.text: Twelve.
Eight.
Fifteen.
Ten.

questions.feedback_correct: The Anti-Federalists lost the argument over the Constitution, but they won a lasting gift for the country.

questions.text: A transportation agency writes rules about how road signs must be posted. Which source of law is this?

answers.text: A regulation.
A statute.
Case law.
The Constitution.

questions.feedback_correct: Regulations are rules made by executive agencies to carry out statutes.

questions.text: Two neighbors go to court over a damaged car. Which kind of law applies?

answers.text: Criminal law.
Civil law.
Military law.
Treaty law.

questions.feedback_correct: In a civil case one side sues another, and the usual result is money or an order to act.

quizzes.title: 9.28 Critical Questions: Brutus No. 1
quizzes.description: Two questions on an essay that argued against the new Constitution. Read the source first.

questions.text: Which two statements would Brutus agree with? Select two.

answers.text: A government over a vast country cannot know the needs of people far away.
A national government with too much power may become a tyranny.
The Constitution should be adopted without debate.
The states are unnecessary.

questions.feedback_correct: He and others who opposed the Constitution wanted a bill of rights and a government close to home.

questions.text: Brutus writes in support of the Constitution as it was drafted in Philadelphia.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: Brutus is an Anti-Federalist. He argues against adopting the Constitution as written.

quizzes.title: Module 9 Outro: Origins
quizzes.description: You have finished this module. Answer honestly. Your answers help your teacher see what is clear and what is not.

quizzes.title: Module 10 Intro: Organization and Citizens
quizzes.description:
In this module you will study how the Constitution is organized. You will ask what each branch does, how the branches and the states check one another, how the Constitution can change, and what rights and duties belong to citizens. These questions come first so that you can see how your answers change by the end.

By the end of this module you will be able to:

  • describe the powers of Congress, the President, and the courts, and explain why the Founders chose three branches;
  • explain checks and balances, judicial review, and the four ways the Constitution limits government;
  • tell delegated, reserved, and concurrent powers apart, and compare federal, unitary, and confederal systems;
  • explain how the Constitution is amended, how Florida’s constitution compares, and which level of government provides which services;
  • tell the duties a citizen owes from the responsibilities a citizen chooses, explain the rights in the Bill of Rights and how the 14th Amendment carried them to the states, and describe how landmark cases and amendments widened the republic.

questions.text: Essential question, first answer. "How does the Constitution divide power, and what keeps each part of government in its place?" Answer in three or four sentences. There is no wrong answer yet. We will ask again at the end.
Objectives. "I have read the module goals above."

answers.text: Yes, I have read them.
I have a question about them. (Say what in the box below.)

questions.text: Question about the goals. If you chose the second answer above, what is your question? Otherwise write "none."
Group work. "Some assessments in this module may be done alone or with a group. If you choose a group, you will sign the Group Covenant first. Which would you like?"

answers.text: I plan to work alone.
I would like to work in a group.
I am not sure yet.

quizzes.title: 10.2 Reading Quiz: Three Branches, Three Jobs
quizzes.description: Five questions on the powers and jobs of Congress, the President, and the courts, and why the Founders divided government into three.

questions.text: Which pair is correct for the Senate?

answers.text: 435 members, two-year terms.
100 members, four-year terms.
100 members, six-year terms.
50 members, one-year terms.

questions.feedback_correct: The Framers meant the House to be close to the people and the Senate to be slower and steadier.

questions.text: How can Congress pass a bill that the President has vetoed?

answers.text: By a two-thirds vote in each house.
By a simple majority in the House.
By a vote of the Supreme Court.
It cannot.

questions.feedback_correct: This is called an override.

questions.text: What happens in an impeachment?

answers.text: The Senate accuses, and the House holds a trial.
The Supreme Court accuses, and the President holds a trial.
The President accuses, and the courts hold a trial.
The House accuses by a majority vote, and the Senate holds a trial where two thirds must vote to convict.

questions.feedback_correct: Impeachment is a check by Congress on the President, judges, and other officials.

questions.text: Why can a President not declare war or raise a tax?

answers.text: The Framers feared a king, so they gave those powers to Congress.
The President is not allowed to command the army.
The Constitution does not mention war or taxes.
The courts make those decisions.

questions.feedback_correct: The President is commander in chief, but war and money belong to Congress.

questions.text: Why do federal judges hold their offices “during good behavior,” usually for life?

answers.text: So that they will have no work to do.
So that they can be removed at each election.
So that they are free from pressure and can rule by the law, not by what is popular.
So that the President can choose them again.

questions.feedback_correct: Judges can still be impeached and removed for wrongdoing.

quizzes.title: 10.4 Critical Questions: Madison, Federalist No. 51
quizzes.description: Two questions on how Madison explained the checks on power. Read the source first.

questions.text: Madison writes, “If men were angels, no government would be necessary.” What does he mean?

answers.text: People are perfect, so we need only a few laws.
Government is not necessary in any country.
Angels should be chosen as rulers.
People are not perfect, so government is needed, and it must be built to restrain itself too.

questions.feedback_correct: The government must first control the governed, and then control itself.

questions.text: According to Madison, ambition in each branch can be used to guard against the other branches taking too much power.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: He writes that “ambition must be made to counteract ambition.”

quizzes.title: 10.7 Reading Quiz: Checks and Balances and the Limits on Government
quizzes.description: Five questions on how each branch checks the others, Marbury v. Madison, and the ways the Constitution limits government.

questions.text: Which of these is a check that Congress has on the President?

answers.text: Declaring a law unconstitutional.
Vetoing a bill.
The Senate must approve many appointments and two thirds must approve a treaty.
Choosing the Chief Justice for life.

questions.feedback_correct: Congress can also override a veto and impeach.

questions.text: What did Chief Justice Marshall decide in Marbury v. Madison?

answers.text: Marbury had a right to his commission, but the Court could not order it, because part of the law of 1789 that gave the Court that power was unconstitutional.
Marbury had no right to his commission, and Madison won.
The Court ordered Madison to deliver the commission at once.
The President could remove any judge he pleased.

questions.feedback_correct: Marshall lost the small battle and won a much larger one.

questions.text: What power did the Court claim in this case?

answers.text: The power to veto a bill.
Judicial review: striking down laws that conflict with the Constitution.
The power to impeach the President.
The power to declare war.

questions.feedback_correct: It was not used again against a federal law for more than fifty years, but it has shaped American government ever since.

questions.text: What does Madison’s phrase “ambition must be made to counteract ambition” mean?

answers.text: Citizens should never be ambitious.
Only one branch should be ambitious.
Leaders in each branch will want to protect their own power, and that desire can be used to guard the Constitution.
Ambition always leads to tyranny.

questions.feedback_correct: If one branch reaches for too much, the others have both the means and the motive to push back.

questions.text: Which of these is one of the four ways the Constitution limits government?

answers.text: Life tenure for the President.
Majority vote on every law.
Rule by the Senate alone.
Due process.

questions.feedback_correct: The four are checks and separated powers, individual rights, the rule of law, and due process.

quizzes.title: 10.8 Critical Questions: Marbury v. Madison (1803)
quizzes.description: Two questions on Chief Justice Marshall’s opinion. Read the source first.

questions.text: Marshall writes that it is “emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” What does this claim?

answers.text: Only the President may interpret the law.
Judges decide what the law means, and may judge whether a law fits the Constitution.
Congress should reread every case.
The courts must follow every order of the President.

questions.feedback_correct: This is the heart of judicial review.

questions.text: According to Marshall, a law that conflicts with the Constitution is still valid until Congress repeals it.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: He writes that a law repugnant to the Constitution is void.

quizzes.title: 10.12 Reading Quiz: Federalism and the Tenth Amendment
quizzes.description: Five questions on how the Constitution divides power between the nation and the states, and how federal, unitary, and confederal systems differ.

questions.text: Which of these is a concurrent power, shared by the nation and the states?

answers.text: Declaring war.
Coining money.
Running most local schools.
Taxing.

questions.feedback_correct: Both the nation and the states may also build roads and set up courts.

questions.text: What does the Supremacy Clause say?

answers.text: When the Constitution, a national law, or a treaty conflicts with a state law, the national law wins.
State laws always win over national laws.
The President may cancel any state law.
The Supreme Court must approve every state law.

questions.feedback_correct: Without this clause, federalism would slide back into the confusion of the Articles.

questions.text: How did Marshall answer the question of whether Congress could create a bank, though the word “bank” is not in the Constitution?

answers.text: The Constitution forbids it.
Only the states may create banks.
Congress has powers over taxes, borrowing, and trade, and under the Necessary and Proper Clause it may choose appropriate means to carry them out.
The President must approve it.

questions.feedback_correct: These are the implied powers.

questions.text: Marshall wrote that “the power to tax involves the power to destroy.” Why did that decide the case?

answers.text: It meant that banks are bad.
It showed that Congress could never tax.
It meant that Maryland needed more money.
If states could tax national agencies, they could destroy the national government itself.

questions.feedback_correct: A state could not tax an agency of the nation.

questions.text: Which system were the Articles of Confederation?

answers.text: A federal system.
A confederal system, where the states held most power.
A unitary system.
A monarchy.

questions.feedback_correct: You have seen how it failed.

quizzes.title: 10.14 Critical Questions: Article IV, Article V, and the Tenth Amendment
quizzes.description: Two questions on how the Constitution treats the states and how it can be amended. Read the source first.

questions.text: The Tenth Amendment says that powers not delegated to the nation, nor prohibited to the states, “are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.” What does this mean for a power the Constitution neither gives to the nation nor forbids to the states?

answers.text: It belongs to the states or to the people.
It belongs to the President.
It belongs to the Supreme Court.
It belongs to no one.

questions.feedback_correct: This is the basis of reserved powers.

questions.text: Article V says that an amendment becomes valid when ratified by the legislatures or conventions of three fourths of the states.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: This is why thirty-eight of fifty states must approve.

quizzes.title: 10.17 Reading Quiz: Amending, Florida, and Government Services
quizzes.description: Five questions on how the Constitution can be amended, how Florida’s constitution compares with the national one, and what each level of government provides.

questions.text: How is an amendment proposed?

answers.text: By a vote of the Supreme Court.
By a majority vote in the Senate.
By the President alone.
By two thirds of both houses of Congress, or by a convention that two thirds of the states ask for.

questions.feedback_correct: The first step is hard on purpose.

questions.text: How many states must ratify an amendment?

answers.text: Thirty-eight of fifty, or three fourths.
Twenty-six of fifty.
All fifty.
Twenty-five of fifty.

questions.feedback_correct: This is why the Constitution has only twenty-seven amendments.

questions.text: What happened to the Equal Rights Amendment?

answers.text: It was ratified in 1972.
It was ratified by all fifty states.
It won approval from thirty-five states, three short of the thirty-eight needed, before its deadline passed.
It was never proposed by Congress.

questions.feedback_correct: An idea must win a large and lasting majority, in many different states.

questions.text: How is Florida’s constitution different from the national one?

answers.text: It does not have a Declaration of Rights.
It begins with a Declaration of Rights, and voters can amend it through routes such as a citizen initiative.
It is shorter than the national Constitution.
It can never be changed.

questions.feedback_correct: Florida’s constitution may give residents more rights than the national one, but never fewer.

questions.text: A pothole has damaged a street near your home. Which office should you contact?

answers.text: The Governor.
Congress.
The city or county public works office.
The Supreme Court.

questions.feedback_correct: A citizen who knows which door to knock on can make government answer.

quizzes.title: 10.18 Critical Questions: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
quizzes.description: Two questions on Chief Justice Marshall’s opinion about the national bank. Read the source first.

questions.text: Which two statements does Marshall make in the opinion? Select two.

answers.text: “The power to tax involves the power to destroy.”
Congress may choose means that are appropriate to a legitimate end, if they fit the letter and spirit of the Constitution.
Congress has only the powers that are listed word for word.
A state may tax any agency of the national government.

questions.feedback_correct: The first answers the question about Maryland’s tax. The second answers the question about the bank.

questions.text: Why does Marshall say that Maryland may not tax the Bank?

answers.text: The Bank was too small to tax.
The Bank belonged to Maryland.
A state that could tax a national agency could destroy it, and the nation must not be at the mercy of the states.
Congress had not created the Bank.

questions.feedback_correct: This protects the national government within its own sphere.

quizzes.title: 10.22 Reading Quiz: Citizens: Rights, Duties, and the Bill of Rights
quizzes.description: Five questions on what a citizen owes the republic, the rights in the Bill of Rights, and how the 14th Amendment carried those rights to the states.

questions.text: Which of these is a duty, something the law requires of a citizen?

answers.text: Volunteering at a food bank.
Voting in every election.
Serving on a jury when called.
Writing to a lawmaker.

questions.feedback_correct: Duties are required by law. Responsibilities, such as voting and volunteering, are chosen by a free citizen.

questions.text: What must police usually have before they search a person’s home?

answers.text: A warrant, signed by a judge, based on good reason.
The permission of a neighbor.
A tip from a newspaper.
A note from the mayor.

questions.feedback_correct: This is the Fourth Amendment’s protection against unreasonable searches and seizures.

questions.text: A woman is found not guilty of a crime, and then the government charges her with the same crime again. Which amendment forbids this?

answers.text: The First Amendment.
The Third Amendment.
The Eighth Amendment.
The Fifth Amendment, which forbids double jeopardy.

questions.feedback_correct: The Fifth also guarantees due process and protects a person from being forced to testify against himself or herself.

questions.text: What does the Ninth Amendment say?

answers.text: Only the rights listed in the Bill of Rights belong to the people.
The people keep other rights even if they are not named in the Constitution.
The states may take away any right they wish.
Soldiers may live in private homes.

questions.feedback_correct: Together with the Tenth, it keeps the Bill of Rights from being read as a complete list of everything a free people may do.

questions.text: What is incorporation?

answers.text: The way a person becomes a citizen after being born in another country.
The vote Congress takes to amend the Constitution.
The process by which the Supreme Court applied most of the Bill of Rights to the states through the 14th Amendment.
The rule that a jury verdict must be unanimous.

questions.feedback_correct: Because of incorporation, a state police officer must follow the Fourth Amendment, and a state court must follow the Sixth.

quizzes.title: 10.24 Critical Questions: The Bill of Rights
quizzes.description: Two questions on the first ten amendments. Read the source first.

questions.text: The Fifth Amendment says that no person “shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself.” What does this protect?

answers.text: The right to a speedy trial.
A person accused of a crime cannot be forced to give evidence that could prove his own guilt.
The right to keep and bear arms.
A person’s right to a jury in civil cases.

questions.feedback_correct: Compare this with the warnings that police must give a suspect before questioning.

questions.text: The Ninth Amendment says that because the Constitution lists certain rights, other rights retained by the people are not denied or disparaged.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: The list is not the whole story. The people keep rights that are not named.

quizzes.title: 10.28 Critical Questions: Miranda v. Arizona (1966)
quizzes.description: Two questions on Chief Justice Warren’s opinion. Read the source first.

questions.text: Which two warnings must a suspect receive before police begin questioning? Select two.

answers.text: He has the right to remain silent.
He must answer every question truthfully.
Anything he says can be used against him in a court of law.
He may have a lawyer only if he can pay for one.

questions.feedback_correct: The opinion also says that he has the right to the presence of an attorney, and that one will be appointed if he cannot afford one.

questions.text: Why does the Court require these warnings?

answers.text: To make police work slower.
To free every person who has confessed.
To give judges the power to question suspects.
To protect the privilege against self-incrimination from the pressure of questioning in custody.

questions.feedback_correct: Miranda was tried again without his confession and convicted anyway. The ruling made sure police follow fair steps.

quizzes.title: Module 11 Intro: Policy and Practice
quizzes.description:
In this module you will study how citizens take part in public policy and how the republic deals with the world. You will follow an election from registration to the count, ask what a citizen can do between elections, look at the republic’s place among other nations, and compare economic systems. You will also practice for the end-of-course exam. These questions come first so that you can see how your answers change by the end.

By the end of this module you will be able to:

  • follow the steps of an election, explain the Electoral College, and tell how the election of 1800 led to the 12th Amendment;
  • explain Madison’s idea of faction and Tocqueville’s view of associations, judge a source for bias, and act on a local problem;
  • describe how America has argued about its place in the world, from Washington’s warning to the Truman Doctrine;
  • compare market, mixed, and command economies, and use GDP per capita as evidence;
  • review the whole course by tracing each part of the Constitution to the failure it answers.

questions.text: Essential question, first answer. "What does it take for citizens to keep a free republic working, at home and in the world?" Answer in three or four sentences. There is no wrong answer yet. We will ask again at the end.
Objectives. "I have read the module goals above."

I have a question about them. (Say what in the box below.)

Group work. "Some assessments in this module may be done alone or with a group. If you choose a group, you will sign the Group Covenant first. Which would you like?"

quizzes.title: 11.2 Reading Quiz: Elections and the Electoral College
quizzes.description: Five questions on how elections work, the Electoral College, and the election of 1800.

questions.text: Who has the main job of running elections in the United States?

answers.text: The President.
The Supreme Court.
The states, under rules that Congress may change.
The United Nations.

questions.feedback_correct: That is why voting rules and ballots differ from place to place.

questions.text: Which set of qualifications fits the office of President?

answers.text: At least twenty-five years old and a citizen for seven years.
At least thirty years old and a citizen for nine years.
At least thirty-five years old, a natural-born citizen, and a resident for fourteen years.
At least twenty-one years old and born in the capital.

questions.feedback_correct: The first set fits a member of the House, and the second fits a senator.

questions.text: In which order do the steps of an election come?

answers.text: Registration, primaries, general election, count.
Primaries, registration, count, general election.
General election, registration, primaries, count.
Count, registration, primaries, general election.

questions.feedback_correct: Each step has rules, and citizens and the press can watch each one.

questions.text: How many electoral votes does a candidate need to win the presidency?
questions.feedback_correct: There are 538 electors in all: one for each member of Congress, plus three for the District of Columbia.

questions.text: Why did Jefferson and Burr tie in the election of 1800?

answers.text: The House refused to count the votes.
Every Republican elector voted for both men, because electors had no separate vote for Vice President.
Burr had won more votes in every state.
The Senate had changed the rules.

questions.feedback_correct: The 12th Amendment fixed the flaw by having electors cast separate votes for President and Vice President.

quizzes.title: 11.4 Critical Questions: Madison, Federalist No. 10
quizzes.description: Two questions on how Madison thought about factions. Read the source first.

questions.text: Madison writes, “Liberty is to faction what air is to fire.” What does he mean?

answers.text: Liberty puts an end to faction.
Faction is the cause of liberty.
Liberty feeds faction, but to abolish liberty in order to remove faction would be a worse mistake.
Faction cannot exist in a republic.

questions.feedback_correct: Madison says it would be as foolish to destroy liberty because it feeds faction as to destroy air because it feeds fire.

questions.text: Madison says that the way to cure faction is to give every citizen the same opinions, passions, and interests, and that this is easy to do.

answers.text: True
False

questions.feedback_correct: Madison calls this cure impracticable. He turns instead to controlling the effects of faction.

quizzes.title: 11.7 Reading Quiz: Media, Interest Groups, and Local Action
quizzes.description: Five questions on Madison and factions, Tocqueville and associations, the press, and acting on a local problem.

questions.text: According to the lesson, why does a large republic help limit the harm of faction?

answers.text: It has fewer people with different interests.
It is hard for any single faction to gain a majority when there are many different groups.
It forbids groups from meeting.
It has one ruler who decides.

questions.feedback_correct: In a small republic, one faction can easily become a majority and rule everyone else.

questions.text: What did Tocqueville notice about Americans?

answers.text: They waited for the government to solve problems.
They did not trust their neighbors.
They often formed groups to work together on almost any purpose.
They let the nobles do most things.

questions.feedback_correct: He believed this habit helped keep the republic free.

questions.text: Which example shows bias in the way a writer describes a plan?

answers.text: Calling the plan “a scheme” instead of “a proposal.”
Giving the date the plan was announced.
Listing who voted for the plan.
Quoting the plan’s text.

questions.feedback_correct: Loaded words can push a reader toward a belief without giving any facts.

questions.text: Which sequence matches the lesson’s method for acting on a local problem?

answers.text: Complain, wait, ask someone else, give up.
Choose an action, research, find the agency, weigh alternatives.
Find the Governor, write to Congress, wait, research.
Research the problem, find the agency in charge, weigh the alternatives, choose an action.

questions.feedback_correct: A street in town belongs to the city or county, not to the Governor or Congress.

questions.text: What is propaganda?

answers.text: A message made to change what people believe or do, often by stirring up feeling instead of giving fair facts.
A law passed by a state legislature.
A neutral report of the day’s weather.
A signed request to the government.

questions.feedback_correct: A careful reader asks who made a message, who it was made for, and what it wants the audience to do.

quizzes.title: 11.8 Critical Questions: Tocqueville, Democracy in America
quizzes.description: Two questions on what Tocqueville saw in American life. Read the source first.

questions.text: Tocqueville writes that “Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions, constantly form associations.” What is he describing?

answers.text: Americans of every kind often join together in groups.
Only the wealthy form groups.
Only the government forms groups.
Americans avoid joining groups.

questions.feedback_correct: He says that where the French would look to the government, Americans form an association.

questions.text: Which two statements agree with the text? Select two.

answers.text: Americans form not only business companies but associations of a thousand other kinds, religious, moral, serious, or silly.
Associations in America are formed only for business.
Where a Frenchman would look to the government, an American is sure to form an association.
Americans leave every new project to a man of rank.

questions.feedback_correct: This habit of working together is one of the ways a free people keeps its freedom.

quizzes.title: 11.12 Reading Quiz: Foreign Policy and International Organizations
quizzes.description: Five questions on how foreign policy connects to life at home, the Monroe Doctrine, the League of Nations, and the Truman Doctrine.

questions.text: What advice did Washington give about alliances?

answers.text: Join every alliance that is offered.
Never trade with other nations.
Deal fairly with all nations, but steer clear of permanent alliances.
Let Congress make every alliance in secret.

questions.feedback_correct: The new republic was weak, and Washington wanted time to grow strong.

questions.text: What did the Monroe Doctrine say?

answers.text: The Americas were no longer open to new colonies from Europe, and the United States would stay out of Europe’s wars.
The United States would take over Spain’s colonies.
The United States would join every European war.
Only Great Britain could settle new land.

questions.text: Why did the United States never join the League of Nations?

answers.text: The League refused to let America in.

The League was shut down before the vote.

questions.text: What is the main promise of NATO?

answers.text: That every member will share one army.
That an attack on one member is an attack on all.
That members will not trade with each other.
That the President may declare war alone.

questions.feedback_correct: The United States and eleven other countries formed NATO in 1949.

questions.text: What did the Truman Doctrine ask Congress to do?

answers.text: Withdraw all troops from Europe.
End the United Nations.
Give money to Greece and Turkey to support free peoples resisting being forced into a communist system.
Declare war on the Soviet Union.

questions.feedback_correct: It set the pattern for years of Cold War policy.

quizzes.title: 11.14 Critical Questions: Monroe, Seventh Annual Message (1823)
quizzes.description: Two questions on President Monroe’s message to Congress. Read the source first.

questions.text: Which two statements does Monroe make? Select two.

answers.text: The United States has not taken part in the wars of European powers in matters relating to themselves.
The United States will join every European war.
Any attempt by Europe to extend its system to this hemisphere would be dangerous to the nation’s peace and safety.
Europe may take back its colonies in the Americas.

questions.feedback_correct: Notice the bargain. The United States stays out of Europe’s quarrels, and Europe stays out of the Americas.

questions.text: Monroe says the American continents are “not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers.” What does this mean?

answers.text: Europeans may settle anywhere they wish.
No European power should start new colonies in the Americas.
The United States will start colonies in Europe.
Colonies must pay taxes to Britain.

questions.feedback_correct: The nations of the Americas had won their independence, and Monroe was warning Europe not to take it back.

quizzes.title: 11.17 Reading Quiz: Capitalism, Command Economies, and Communism
quizzes.description: Five questions on market, mixed, and command economies, what communism did, and GDP per capita.

questions.text: In a market economy, who decides what to make and sell?

answers.text: Government officials.
A single ruling party.
The United Nations.
Private people and businesses, guided by prices.

questions.feedback_correct: Prices rise when something is scarce and drop when it is plentiful, and these signals tell producers what to make.

questions.text: Which of these describes a mixed economy such as that of the United States?

answers.text: The government owns almost every farm and factory.
Most of the economy is private, but government builds roads and schools, enforces contracts, and regulates unfair competition.
There are no taxes.
Prices are set only by the government.

questions.feedback_correct: A free market is not a market without rules. It is a market under law.

questions.text: What does the lesson give as the cause of the famines in the Soviet Union and China?

answers.text: Bad weather alone.
Too many private farms.
Orders from the government that no one could question, such as forcing farmers onto state-run farms.
Too much trade with other countries.

questions.text: What does China’s story after 1978 show?

answers.text: Markets raise incomes, but the freedom to speak and vote is a separate matter that markets alone do not guarantee.

Command economies always grow faster.
Private business causes famine.
