quizzes.title: 11.31 Quarter 4 Exam: The Republic Reviewed
quizzes.description: Forty multiple-choice questions on this quarter’s work: the roots of American government, the Founding, how the Constitution is organized, rights and cases, elections, and the republic’s place in the world. Work alone and without notes. You have one attempt.

questions.text: Which Roman idea is a root of the rule of law?

answers.text: Written laws known in advance that bind everyone, such as the Twelve Tables.
Rule by a single king whose word is the law, so that no one else has to write laws down.
Laws kept secret by the nobles, so that only the judges of the city can know what they are.
Rule by whichever general commands the largest army, as in the last years of the Republic.

questions.text: Which ancient place gave the Founders the idea that law stands above kings?

answers.text: Sparta, in the story of its two kings and its council.
Jerusalem, in the story of King David and the prophet Nathan.
Persia, in the story of its emperor and his governors.
Egypt, in the story of its pharaohs and their priests.

questions.text: What did the clause in Magna Carta about a “lawful judgment” begin?

answers.text: The right of every adult to vote, which later spread from England to the American colonies.
The idea of due process, that a ruler must follow the law before punishing someone.
The power of judicial review, which let English judges strike down the king’s orders.
The Electoral College, which the English used to choose their kings after John.

questions.text: Why is the Mayflower Compact an early example of government by consent?

answers.text: The king wrote it for the colony, and the passengers agreed to it only after they reached shore.
It set up a Parliament of the colonists, with a House of Lords chosen by the king.
Every person in England signed it before the ship sailed, so the whole nation consented.
The signers made their own government by agreeing together, and no king gave it to them.

questions.text: Why is the Glorious Revolution called “glorious”?

answers.text: It changed the government with little bloodshed, and Parliament then set limits on the Crown.
It ended every tax in England, and the new king ruled without any Parliament at all.
It crowned a king for life, and it gave him the power to make laws on his own.
It made England a republic, and the monarchy was abolished for the next hundred years.

questions.text: How did Locke’s view of government differ from Hobbes’s?

answers.text: Locke wanted a king with unlimited power, while Hobbes wanted a republic with a written constitution.
Both said that government has no purpose, and they differed only on how to end it.
Locke said rights come from the ruler, while Hobbes said they come from the people.
Locke said people have natural rights that government must protect, while Hobbes wanted a ruler with almost unlimited power.

questions.text: Why did Montesquieu say the three jobs of government should be in different hands?

answers.text: It makes the government cheaper to run, because each branch can share the same buildings.
When one person or group makes, carries out, and judges the laws, liberty is lost.
It makes laws pass faster, because fewer people have to agree on each one.
It gives the people no voice, so the government can act in secret without fear of the voters.

questions.text: In the Declaration of Independence, what comes after the statement of principles?

answers.text: A plan for the Articles of Confederation, set out article by article for the thirteen states.
A treaty with France, offered in exchange for money and ships to fight the war.
A bill of rights, listing the freedoms of speech, of religion, and of the press.
A list of grievances, offered as proof that the king broke the contract that made his rule just.

questions.text: Why does the lesson call the Olive Branch Petition a “road not taken”?

answers.text: The colonists never sent it, and so the king never learned that they wanted peace.
The king accepted it at once, and the colonies then returned to peaceful British rule.
It asked for independence, and the king rejected it as he did every demand for freedom.
The king refused even to read it, and had he listened, he might have kept the colonies.

questions.text: Which charge in the Declaration violated the principle of consent of the governed?

answers.text: Imposing taxes on the colonists without their consent.
Closing every church in the colonies during the long winter of 1775.
Forbidding the colonists to print books or to read newspapers in their own homes.
Refusing to trade with France, which was then the colonists’ best customer.

questions.text: Which pairing correctly matches a weakness of the Articles of Confederation with its remedy in the Constitution?

answers.text: No national courts: Article II creates a President.
No power to tax: Article III creates the courts.
Hard to amend: Article I gives the President a veto.
No executive: Article II creates a President.

questions.text: Why do the votes in Virginia (89 to 79) and New York (30 to 27) matter?

answers.text: They show that ratification was easy, since each state approved the Constitution by a wide margin.
Any one state could have said no and the nation might have split, and a promise of a bill of rights carried the day.
They show that the Anti-Federalists won, since they carried both states in the end.
They show that the Constitution was rewritten before it was ratified, to answer every critic.

questions.text: What did the Anti-Federalists say the Constitution lacked?

answers.text: A President to carry out the laws.
A Congress to make the laws.
A bill of rights to protect individual citizens.
A Supreme Court to judge the laws.

questions.text: Which is the highest source of law in the United States?

answers.text: The Constitution.
A regulation.
A statute.
Case law.

questions.text: What is a precedent?

answers.text: A law that Congress passes with the approval of the President in the same year.
An earlier court decision that judges use as a guide in later, similar cases.
A rule that an agency writes to carry out a law that the legislature has passed.
A vote of a grand jury on whether a person must stand trial for a serious crime.

questions.text: Who must approve a treaty the President makes?

answers.text: A majority of the House.
The Supreme Court.
Two thirds of the Senate.
The governors of the states.

questions.text: Which is a check that the Senate has on the courts?

answers.text: Overturning a court’s decision by a simple voice vote of the senators present on that day.
Choosing the members of every jury that sits in a federal trial anywhere in the country.
Setting the salary of each federal judge anew at the start of every year of service.
Confirming the President’s choices for federal judges.

questions.text: How did Marshall’s decision in Marbury v. Madison avoid an order that the President might defy?

answers.text: He ordered Madison to deliver the commission and asked the army to see that the order was carried out.
He refused to hear the case at all, and he sent it back to Congress to be decided by a vote.
He said Marbury had a right to his commission but the Court could not order it, because part of a law of 1789 was unconstitutional.
He ruled that Marbury had no right to the commission, and Jefferson then named him to another office.

questions.text: Which is an example of judicial review?

answers.text: The President vetoes a bill that Congress has passed.
The Senate confirms an ambassador chosen by the President.
A court declares a law of Congress unconstitutional.
The House votes to impeach a federal official.

questions.text: The President vetoes a bill that both houses of Congress passed. What can Congress do?

answers.text: Override the veto with a two-thirds vote in each house.
Pass the bill again with a simple majority of both houses and send it back to the President.
Ask the Supreme Court to sign the bill so that it becomes law without the President.
Nothing at all, because under the Constitution a veto can never be overridden.

questions.text: Both the nation and the states may tax, build roads, and set up courts. What kind of power is this?

answers.text: Reserved power.
Delegated power.
Concurrent power.
Implied power.

questions.text: A state law conflicts with a national law. Which wins, and why?

answers.text: The national law, because of the Supremacy Clause.
The state law, because of the Tenth Amendment.
Whichever was passed first, because of the rule of precedent.
Neither, until the people of the state vote on the question.

questions.text: What are implied powers?

answers.text: Powers not listed in the Constitution but reasonably needed to carry out the ones that are listed.
Powers that the states keep for themselves, since the Constitution does not give them away.
Powers that belong to the President alone, since the Constitution says nothing about them.
Powers that were once in the Constitution but have since been taken away by an amendment.

questions.text: Why does the Constitution have only twenty-seven amendments?

answers.text: The Supreme Court limits how many amendments the people may add to the Constitution.
The President decides which amendments the states may be asked to vote on each year.
An amendment needs two thirds of Congress and three fourths of the states, which is hard on purpose.
Every amendment is repealed after ten years unless the states vote to renew it.

questions.text: Which level of government mainly uses property taxes to pay for local schools, police, and fire protection?

answers.text: The national government.
Local governments.
The Supreme Court.
The United Nations.

questions.text: Which amendment forbids unreasonable searches and says police must usually have a warrant?

answers.text: The Second Amendment.
The Sixth Amendment.
The Fourth Amendment.
The Ninth Amendment.

questions.text: What did the Court decide in Gideon v. Wainwright?

answers.text: A state may refuse a lawyer to a poor person, since the Sixth Amendment binds only the nation.
A state must provide a lawyer to a poor person charged with a serious crime.
A confession must be thrown out of court unless the suspect has first been read his rights.
A jury must be chosen by the judge, and neither side may question the people in the pool.

questions.text: What did Brown v. Board of Education decide?

answers.text: Separate public schools are inherently unequal, which overturned Plessy in schools.
Separate public schools are allowed if the buildings and books are equal in every way.
Each school district may decide for itself whether to separate its students by race.
Plessy v. Ferguson was upheld, and segregated schools were declared lawful in every state.

questions.text: What did Justice Harlan say in his lone dissent in Plessy v. Ferguson?

answers.text: That the law was fair, because railway cars for each race were equal in every respect.
That Louisiana could pass any law it wished about its railroads, free of the Constitution.
That the Court should not hear the case, since no one had been hurt by the Louisiana law.
That the Constitution is color-blind and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.

questions.text: Which case held that a state could not make a woman choose between her faith and her unemployment benefits?

answers.text: Lemon v. Kurtzman.
Sherbert v. Verner.
Terry v. Ohio.
Miranda v. Arizona.

questions.text: How many electors does each state have?

answers.text: As many as its members of Congress, in the House and the Senate together.
One for each county in the state, as counted by the most recent census of the people.
Exactly three, no matter how large or how small the population of the state may be.
As many as its members in the House only, with no electors for its senators.

questions.text: Madison says there are two ways to cure faction. Why does he reject them?

answers.text: Both are too costly, and a republic could not raise enough taxes to carry either one out.
Both are forbidden by the Constitution, which says no group may ever be broken up.
Both would make factions larger, because the people would then join together against the government.
One would destroy liberty, and the other would need everyone to think alike, which cannot be done.

questions.text: Why did Tocqueville think American associations helped keep the republic free?

answers.text: They made elections unnecessary, since the groups chose every leader without a vote.
They let the government pick the leaders of each group, so that no one could oppose the law.
Citizens who work together do not wait for a ruler to solve their problems.
They were required by law, and every citizen had to join one or pay a fine to the state.

questions.text: Which is the best example of a citizen acting on a local problem?

answers.text: Posting an angry complaint online without naming any agency or asking for any particular change.
Waiting for the Governor to notice the problem and to send help to the town without being asked.
Gathering facts about accidents at a crossing, finding the agency in charge, and asking it for a specific change.
Writing to Congress about a dangerous street that lies wholly inside one town in one state.

questions.text: Which statement best compares the Monroe Doctrine with the Truman Doctrine?

answers.text: Monroe closed the Americas to new European colonies, and Truman pledged support for free peoples resisting a forced communist system.
Both pledged to stay out of every foreign conflict, and both asked the Senate to reject every treaty.
Monroe founded NATO to defend Europe, and Truman founded the League of Nations to keep the peace.
Monroe offered aid to Greece and Turkey, and Truman closed the Americas to European colonies.

questions.text: Which part of the national government has the power to declare war?

answers.text: The President alone.
Congress.
The Supreme Court.
The United Nations.

questions.text: What is communism, as the lesson describes it?

answers.text: A system in which private businesses and buyers make every decision with no rules from the government.
A system in which a king owns all the land and lends it to farmers in return for their loyalty.
A system in which the states control the army and the national government controls the farms.
A system in which the government, under one ruling party, owns the farms and factories and controls the economy.

questions.text: Why is GDP per capita useful but limited?

answers.text: It measures freedom exactly, so no other figure is needed to compare how well people live.
It counts only the goods the government makes, and it leaves out everything made by private firms.
It cannot be used to compare countries, since each country counts its own money in a different way.
It lets us compare how much each person receives, but it leaves out things such as health and freedom.

questions.text: The Preamble says “insure domestic Tranquility.” Which failure of the Articles does this answer?

answers.text: The states taxed one another’s goods as if they were foreign nations.
Shays’ Rebellion showed that the government could not keep the peace at home.
There were no national courts to settle quarrels between the states.
The Articles could not be amended unless every state agreed.

questions.text: What made the difference between the American republic of 1800 and the German republic of 1933?

answers.text: America had a written constitution and Germany had none, so Germany had no rules to abandon.
Germany held no elections after 1919, and America held elections every year without fail.
Americans divided power, protected rights, and accepted an election’s result, while many Germans abandoned the rules in a crisis.
America had no political parties and Germany had too many, so only Germany lost its republic.

quizzes.title: Module 11 Outro: Policy and Practice
quizzes.description: You have finished this module. Answer honestly. Your answers help your teacher see what is clear and what is not.

questions.text: Essential question, revisited. "What does it take for citizens to keep a free republic working, at home and in the world?" Answer in four or five sentences. Use at least one example from the module (for example the election of 1800, Madison on factions, the Senate’s vote on the League of Nations, or the comparison of North and South Korea). How is your answer different from the one you gave at the start?
Confidence. "How well could you explain this module's main ideas to a classmate?"

answers.text: 5: Very well. I could teach it.
4: Well, with one or two gaps.
3: Somewhat. I need to review a few parts.
2: Not very well.
1: Not at all.

questions.text: What is still unclear. "Name one idea, event, or term from this module that is still unclear to you. If nothing is unclear, say what you would like to learn more about."

answers.text: Courage (for example Justice Harlan writing a lone dissent)
Honesty (for example a careful reader who checks a source for bias)

questions.text: Virtue reflection. "Explain your choice in two or three sentences. Then name one place in your own life where this virtue will be asked of you."

discussions.title: 6.10 Discussion: Who Should Be a Citizen?
discussions.html:
Make a claim about what should make a person a citizen of a republic. You might focus on birth, parentage, naturalization, or something else. Support your claim with at least one example from this module's lessons (for example Dred Scott, the 14th Amendment, Wong Kim Ark, the Chinese Exclusion Act, or the territories). Then say one thing a citizen owes the republic, and whether your rule for who counts as a citizen changes what is owed.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Scoring: Substantive = full credit (clear claim, a specific example from the lessons, a reply that engages the classmate's reasoning). Thin = partial credit. Missing = zero.

discussions.title: 6.20 Discussion: Why Did Widening the Vote Take So Long?
discussions.html:
It took from 1870 to 1971 for the amendments on race, sex, poll taxes, and age to widen the vote. Choose one main reason you think it took so long, and support it with evidence from at least two of the amendments you studied (the 15th, 19th, 24th, and 26th). Then answer the lesson's own question: was the slow pace a fault of the system or a safeguard? Give one reason for your answer.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Scoring: Substantive = full credit (a clear reason, evidence from two amendments, a stand on fault or safeguard, a reply that engages the classmate). Thin = partial credit. Missing = zero.

discussions.title: 6.30 Discussion: The Election of 1800: Could the Republic Have Broken?
discussions.html:
In 1800 the House voted thirty-six times before it chose a President. Name the single choice by one person or group that you think mattered most in keeping the republic together: Burr staying quiet, Hamilton writing his letters, the Federalists leaving their ballots blank on the last vote, Adams leaving Washington, or another choice from the lesson. Explain what might have happened if that person or group had chosen differently. Use at least one fact from the lesson.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Scoring: Substantive = full credit (a named choice, a reasoned "what if," a fact from the lesson, a reply that engages the classmate). Thin = partial credit. Missing = zero.

discussions.title: 6.40 Discussion: The Sedition Act: Protection or Censorship?
discussions.html:
Congress said the Sedition Act protected a young country at a time of war scare. Critics said it punished the government's enemies. Take a side: was the Act protection or censorship? Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons (for example who was tried under it, what the law left out, how Jefferson and Madison answered, or how the Zenger trial compares). Then say one thing a citizen should do when a government says a law is needed for safety but the law seems to silence critics.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Scoring: Substantive = full credit (a clear side, two facts from the lessons, a citizen's response, a reply that engages the classmate). Thin = partial credit. Missing = zero.

discussions.title: 6.50 Discussion: Who Should Decide: State or Nation?
discussions.html:
Pick one kind of decision from this module's lessons (for example schools, roads, local crime, family law, defense, money, or the rules of an election). Make a claim about whether the state or the nation should decide it. Use at least one of Madison's reasons for dividing power, which are self-government close to home and safety from too much power in one set of hands, or a fact from the lessons about who provides which service. Then say one thing that could go wrong if the other level decided instead.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

Scoring: Substantive = full credit (a clear claim, one reason or fact from the lessons, one risk of the other choice, a reply that engages the classmate). Thin = partial credit. Missing = zero.

discussions.title: 7.10 Discussion: Hamilton’s Debt Plan: Fair to Whom?
discussions.html:
Hamilton asked Congress to pay the national debt in full and to take over the debts of the states. Some states had already paid most of their debts, and speculators had bought old promises from poor soldiers at low prices. Choose one group affected by the plan (for example soldiers, states that had paid, speculators, or taxpayers) and make a claim about whether the plan was fair to that group. Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons or from Hamilton’s report. Then say one change you would make to the plan, and what it would cost.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 7.20 Discussion: Should Government Break Up Big Business?
discussions.html:
Roosevelt’s government broke Standard Oil into more than thirty companies. Some said that big companies are more efficient and lower prices. Others said that a company which can crush every rival will not keep prices low for long. Take a side: should the government break up a business that has grown very large? Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons, such as Smith’s idea of competition, what Standard Oil did to rivals, or what happened after the breakup. Then state the strongest argument for the other side, and say what evidence would help to decide between you.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 7.30 Discussion: Which System Raises the Standard of Living?
discussions.html:
Make a claim about which kind of economy, market or command, better raises the standard of living. Use at least one comparison from the lessons, such as West and East Germany, South and North Korea, or GDP per capita figures for different countries. Then name one thing that GDP per capita does not measure, and say whether it changes your answer. End with one thing a market cannot do alone, and who in a republic should decide how to handle it.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 8.10 Discussion: Could Weimar Have Been Saved?
discussions.html:
The lessons say that Weimar did not fail by fate, and that its leaders made choices. Name one choice made by a particular person or group in the years before 1933, and say what a different choice would have looked like. Do you think it would have been enough to save the republic? Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons. Then say one thing that a citizen of a republic today can do to keep a republic alive.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 9.10 Discussion: What Did America Inherit?
discussions.html:
The lessons trace American ideas back to Athens, Rome, Jerusalem, Magna Carta, the Mayflower Compact, the English Bill of Rights, and Thomas Paine. Choose one of these that you think matters most to a citizen today, and make a claim about why. Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons. Then name one way that the same place or document failed or fell short, and say how the Founders tried to repair it.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 9.20 Discussion: Were the Colonists’ Grievances Natural-Rights Violations?
discussions.html:
The Declaration lists grievances against the king, and each one says that a right was violated. Choose one grievance and make a claim about whether it really violated a natural right such as life, liberty, or property. Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons. Then say whether you think this grievance, by itself, was serious enough to justify independence, remembering Locke’s warning that people should not change governments for light and passing causes.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 9.30 Discussion: Federalists or Anti-Federalists: Who Was Right About a Bill of Rights?
discussions.html:
The Federalists said that a bill of rights was not needed, because the national government had only listed powers. The Anti-Federalists said that a list of rights was needed to guard against tyranny. Take a side: who was right? Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons, such as the close votes or the promise made to win Virginia and New York. Then state the strongest argument for the other side.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 10.10 Discussion: Do Checks and Balances Still Work?
discussions.html:
Madison wrote that “ambition must be made to counteract ambition.” Choose one check from the lessons, such as the veto, the override, impeachment, Senate approval, or judicial review, and make a claim about whether it still works to keep a branch from taking too much power. Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons, such as Marbury v. Madison. Then say what citizens must do for the checks to work.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 10.20 Discussion: Where Does State Power End?
discussions.html:
McCulloch v. Maryland said that Congress has implied powers and that a state cannot tax the national government. The Tenth Amendment says that other powers are reserved to the states or to the people. Choose one service from the lessons, such as schools, roads, or defense, and make a claim about which level of government should be in charge of it. Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons. Then say what would be lost if the other level held the power.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 10.30 Discussion: Which Right Matters Most to a Free Republic?
discussions.html:
The Bill of Rights protects many freedoms, among them religion, speech and the press, the rights of the accused, and protection from unreasonable searches. Choose the one right you think a free republic could least afford to lose, and make a claim about why. Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons, such as a landmark case or the way a right was carried to the states. Then say what would happen to the other rights if the one you chose were taken away.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 11.10 Discussion: How Should a Citizen Try to Change a Law?
discussions.html:
Suppose there is a local rule that you think is unfair or a problem near your school that needs fixing. Choose one way a citizen can act, such as writing to an official, speaking at a public meeting, starting a petition, joining or forming a group, or voting, and make a claim about why it is the best first step. Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons, such as Madison on factions or Tocqueville on associations. Then say who the citizen should ask, and what specific thing the citizen should ask for.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 11.20 Discussion: Should America Lead the World?
discussions.html:
Washington warned against permanent alliances, and America later helped found the United Nations and NATO. Take a side: should America lead the world, or should it be careful about its commitments? Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons, such as the Senate’s vote on the League of Nations, the Monroe Doctrine, or the Truman Doctrine. Then state the strongest argument for the other side, and say what evidence would help decide between you.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.

discussions.title: 11.30 Discussion: Which Part of the Constitution Answers Which Failure?
discussions.html:
The Constitution was built to answer failures that earlier governments had shown. Choose three parts of the Constitution or the Bill of Rights, and for each one name the failure it answers and one example from the course. Then say which of the three you think a republic most needs in a time of crisis, and why. Support your claim with at least two facts from the lessons, such as the republic of 1800 or the republic of 1933.

Then reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a point of your own. If not, respectfully explain where you think it falls short.
